title: Multiscale Schmidt-Spectrum Bounds For High-Dimensional Entanglement: Geometric Measures And Schmidt-Number Witnesses
authors: Liang Xiong, Zhixiang Jin, Yanling Wang, Wei Chen, Hong Tao, Nung-Sing Sze
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: High-dimensional bipartite entanglement depends on how probability is distributed across the Schmidt spectrum, whereas a single reference-state fidelity resolves only one spectral scale. We develop multiscale Schmidt-spectrum bounds that connect geometric measures with quantitative Schmidt-number witnesses. For any partition of a pure-state Schmidt spectrum, several nested Vidal tails determine block masses. We derive the sharp upper boundary of the associated normalized nuclear-norm coordinate and show that equality holds if and only if the spectrum is uniform within each block. Refining the partition gives a monotone hierarchy of tighter bounds whenever the added tail data distinguish unequal block means. We also solve a relaxed weighted multiscale optimization globally: one scalar parameter specifies its unique full-support optimizer and explicit value on the nontrivial branch. Using the established single-tail fidelity--resource curve as a baseline, we obtain exact-fidelity equality refinements, convex-roof lower bounds for mixed states, and quantitative calibrations of Schmidt-number witnesses. A higher-tail relation further bounds convex-roof extended negativity in terms of Vidal tails and identifies the pure-state equality spectra. Leakage-aware and joint-confidence formulations state how these bounds can be used with incomplete data. Multistep tails require block-resolved or independently certified spectral information; they are not determined by one projector expectation.
tldr: The paper develops multiscale Schmidt-spectrum bounds that connect geometric entanglement measures with quantitative Schmidt-number witnesses for high-dimensional bipartite entanglement.
motivation: High-dimensional entanglement cannot be fully characterized by a single reference-state fidelity because it depends on the distribution of probability across the entire Schmidt spectrum.
method: The authors partition pure-state Schmidt spectra into blocks, use nested Vidal tails to bound block masses, solve a relaxed weighted multiscale optimization globally, and derive convex-roof lower bounds and witness calibrations.
result: They obtain sharp upper boundaries for normalized nuclear-norm coordinates, equality conditions for block-uniform spectra, a monotone hierarchy of tighter bounds, exact-fidelity refinements, and bounds on convex-roof extended negativity via higher-tail relations.
conclusion: The framework provides a systematic way to quantify high-dimensional entanglement and calibrate Schmidt-number witnesses, but multistep tails require block-resolved or independently certified spectral information.

title: Nonlocal Magic Spreading In Many-body Quantum Dynamics: From Chaotic Evolution To Quasi-particle Picture In Integrable Models
authors: Sreemayee Aditya, Piotr Sierant, Xhek Turkeshi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20951v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Entanglement and magic are resources that reveal complementary aspects of quantum many-body systems. Their interplay is captured by nonlocal magic, the magic that survives arbitrary local changes of basis. Yet their markedly different dynamical behavior leaves open how this irreducible component of magic spreads. Here we connect nonlocal magic to the capacity of entanglement, a tractable quantity measuring fluctuations of the entanglement Hamiltonian. This connection enables analytically controlled predictions across a wide range of many-body dynamics, from chaotic to integrable systems, which we investigate also using large-scale numerical simulations. In chaotic systems, nonlocal magic exhibits a transient buildup, with logarithmic growth in time followed by decay to a size-independent value. For integrable systems, we develop a quasiparticle picture in quantitative agreement with numerics, showing that the same initial growth instead leads to saturation at a value logarithmic in subsystem size. These contrasting behaviors have an operational consequence for entanglement embezzlement: the strongest scramblers embezzle only transiently, whereas free-fermionic dynamics can sustain universal embezzlement in the steady state.
tldr: The paper links nonlocal magic to the capacity of entanglement and shows distinct spreading behaviors in chaotic versus integrable many-body quantum dynamics, with implications for entanglement embezzlement.
motivation: Entanglement and magic reveal complementary aspects of quantum many-body systems, but how the nonlocal, basis-independent component of magic spreads dynamically was not well understood.
method: The authors connect nonlocal magic to the capacity of entanglement, enabling analytically controlled predictions across chaotic and integrable dynamics, supported by large-scale numerical simulations.
result: In chaotic systems, nonlocal magic grows logarithmically in time, then decays to a size-independent value; in integrable systems, a quasiparticle picture predicts saturation at a value logarithmic in subsystem size.
conclusion: These contrasting behaviors imply that the strongest scramblers embezzle entanglement only transiently, while free-fermionic dynamics can sustain universal embezzlement in the steady state.

title: Robust Many-body Quantum Batteries
authors: Finn Schmolke, Karen Hovhannisyan, Milton Aguilar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Realistic work extraction from many-body quantum batteries must be local. However, only a small fraction of energy eigenstates of a generic many-body system, called scars, can support local extraction. The remaining bulk is useless for the task due to the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Here we devise a universal low-complexity protocol that steers any initial state towards exactly one scar---representing a charged state of the battery---from which a macroscopic amount of work can be extracted using local unitary operations. This is achieved by leveraging the nontrivial interplay of engineered dissipation and continuous indirect measurement that, in addition, leads to enhanced stability and charging speed compared to any other strategy using these processes independently. Moreover, the protocol works directly on the hardware level, in that it requires no simulation or suppression of interactions between subsystems. Our construction thereby enables macroscopic charge storage in steady states of generic nonintegrable many-body systems indefinitely, from which a reliable stream of work can be extracted via purely local means.
tldr: A universal low-complexity protocol steers generic many-body quantum battery states into a single scar via engineered dissipation and continuous measurement, enabling macroscopic local work extraction with enhanced stability and charging speed.
motivation: Realistic work extraction from many-body quantum batteries must be local, but the eigenstate thermalization hypothesis makes most eigenstates useless for this task except for special scar states.
method: The protocol combines engineered dissipation and continuous indirect measurement to steer any initial state toward exactly one scar, without requiring simulation or suppression of interactions between subsystems.
result: It achieves macroscopic charge storage in steady states of generic nonintegrable many-body systems indefinitely, with reliable local work extraction and improved stability and charging speed compared to using dissipation or measurement independently.
conclusion: This enables robust many-body quantum batteries that operate directly at the hardware level and overcome generic thermalization limitations for sustained work extraction.

title: Polariton Bell Node For Quantum Repeaters
authors: Alexey Kavokin Junhui Cao
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a Bell-measurement node for quantum repeaters based on a planar semiconductor microcavity operating in the strong-coupling regime. Cavity photons hybridize with quantum-well excitons to form polaritons combining properties of photons and matter quasiparticles. A control photon loaded into one polariton mode changes the polarization response seen by a subsequently incident target photon. This conditional rotation is governed by the interplay of self-induced Larmor precession triggered by spin-dependent exciton-exciton interactions and the polarization beats caused by the splitting of transverse-electric and transverse-magnetic cavity modes. We identify conditions of the experiment that enable implementation of a controlled-Z gate and allow to distinguish all four Bell states in the ideal limit. The one-sided scattering scheme provides a lower interaction threshold than a scalar Kerr reference under the same assumptions. At a selected operating point, the bandwidth-induced identification error scales as the fourth power of the pulse bandwidth in the narrow-band limit. An additional fixed input rotation reduces this error even further. We describe the entanglement swapping between remote memories and determine the minimum quality of the elementary links needed to obtain an entangled output.

motivation: Quantum repeaters require efficient Bell measurements and entanglement swapping, and new physical implementations could lower interaction thresholds and improve scalability.
method: The scheme uses a planar semiconductor microcavity in the strong-coupling regime, where cavity photons hybridize with quantum-well excitons to form polaritons; conditional rotation arises from self-induced Larmor precession and TE-TM mode splitting.
result: The authors identify operating conditions for a controlled-Z gate and Bell state discrimination, show that bandwidth-induced identification error scales as the fourth power of pulse bandwidth in the narrow-band limit, and demonstrate that an additional fixed input rotation further reduces this error.
conclusion: The polariton Bell node may provide a lower interaction threshold than a scalar Kerr reference and can support entanglement swapping between remote memories, with determined minimum elementary link quality for entangled output.

title: ReFINE: Scheduling Of Distillation And Coding For Rate-Fidelity Tradeoff In Quantum Networks
authors: Narges Alavisamani, Matthieu Bloch, Moinuddin Qureshi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In quantum networks, nodes are connected via sharing of Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen (EPR) pairs, ideally with high fidelity and high rate. However, the fidelity of EPR pairs degrades due to imperfect generation and decoherence errors. Entanglement Distillation is a method that increases the fidelity but operates probabilistically and may destroy all involved EPR pairs upon failure. This failure reduces available EPR pairs for application use, thereby decreasing the service rate. Quantum Error Correction (QEC) is another mechanism to protect EPR pairs against error by forming what we term as Coding-Enhanced Memory (CEM). While effective, CEM requires extra time and resources to form the code, which also reduces the service rate. Existing methods often use static combinations of distillation and CEM, ignoring demand variations. This results in a low service rate without significant fidelity gain. Limited resources together with this rate-fidelity tradeoff make it essential to schedule when to run distillation, form CEM, or serve requests. We propose ReFINE, a demand-aware preemptive scheduler that based on application requirements either serves an available EPR pair immediately or preserves it in CEM. This selective use of CEM, only when needed, enables a better balance for rate-fidelity tradeoff than always using CEM. Between request arrivals, ReFINE either schedules distilling EPR pairs or forming CEM to protect distilled pairs, following one of the three priority policies: ReFINE-D (Distillation-First) first generates EPR pairs for distillation and then forms the CEM, prioritizing service rate. ReFINE-M (Memory-First) first forms the CEM, then generates the EPR pairs for distillation, prioritizing fidelity. ReFINE-C (Concurrent) performs both distillation and CEM formation concurrently, balancing between fidelity and service rate.

title: Commutator Geometry And Information Preservation In The Quantum Switch

abstract: ArXiv:2609.21310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Two commuting channels yield the same composite channel in either fixed order, yet their quantum switch can alter information preservation. The reverse inequality holds for pure states of two qubits whose control Schmidt basis can be chosen to coincide with the order basis. A commutator matrix determines the target basis that maximizes the squared fidelity gap at fixed entanglement within this aligned family. For Pauli [MATH] and [MATH] channels with equal error probabilities, the switch replaces a logical phase flip with an operator that stabilizes a joint code. At fixed noise, the switch preserves at least as much distinguishability and quantum Fisher information as fixed order for every state family in this code. For the pure encoded family studied here, exact formulas connect the phase information gain to the squared fidelity gap and quantify the reduction in information about the noise probability. Optimizing the probes yields equal maximal quantum Fisher information for noise estimation under both joint channels. These results connect commutator geometry and logical error structure to state preservation and the retention of encoded information.

title: A Memory-information Window In Finite-duration Quantum Control
authors: Ahn Doyeol (david)
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21380v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Environmental noise is a major source of decoherence and errors in quantum systems. In a non-Markovian environment, the noise has a finite correlation time, and the system can retain information about its previous interactions with the environment. Simulations at different gate durations tg further show that the information window approximately follows the dimensionless correlation ratio {\tau}c/tg. These results provide a timescale-matching principle for probing finite-correlation non-Markovian noise with coherent quantum control.

title: Local Detailed Balance In The Lorenz Model: Replaces The Butterfly With Frenetic Bursting
authors: Christian Maes Faezeh Khodabandehlou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Lorenz system is the canonical low-order model of convective instability, yet its dissipative and driving terms have never been checked against, nor constructed from, an explicit thermodynamic bookkeeping. The resulting model produces a transition from a quiescent fixed point to a robust, large-amplitude relaxation oscillation, closely analogous to recharge-discharge oscillator paradigms used for the El Nino-Southern Oscillation. title: Giant-Atom-Induced High-Order Output Zeros In A Coupled-Cavity Array
authors: Mengxue Li, Bo Liu, H. Z. Shen, H. D. Liu, Gangcheng Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coherent perfect absorption, zero transmission and zero reflection are several scattering phenomena governed by interference engineering in Hermitian and non-Hermitian systems. Higher-order coherent perfect absorption can significantly broaden the absorption bandwidth, while existing implementations rely on scattering zero degeneracy induced by exceptional points or additional momentum-dependent phase delays introduced in incident waves. We propose a scheme where a giant atom couples to a one-dimensional coupled-cavity array at two spatially separated sites. The spatially separated coupling configuration of the giant atom generates tunable nonlocal interference phases that dominate the scattering interference process. We further investigate the zero-reflection and zero-transmission behaviors under single-sided incidence. Our results reveal that the giant-atom interference mechanism enables bandwidth-enhanced coherent perfect absorption and bandwidth-enhanced zero transmission in the absence of exceptional points and incident momentum-dependent phase delays. Our work provides a physical route for coherent wave manipulation in coupled-cavity quantum networks.

title: Passive Pauli Toggling Of Polarization Qubits In Optical Fibers: Error Bounds And Qkd Performance
authors: Jeongho Bang Bongjune Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polarization qubits offer a direct route to fiber-based quantum communication, yet the fiber that carries them also scrambles their reference frame through uncontrolled birefringence. Active compensation commonly relies on monitoring and feedback, raising a natural question: can the link itself suppress coherent polarization drift before it reaches the receiver? We show that it can within a regime of sufficiently correlated unitary drift. Our central idea is to embed a fixed cyclic sequence of Pauli rotations along the fiber, turning propagation distance into a spatial toggling frame. Rather than estimating and inverting the unknown transformation, the sequence repeatedly reverses its leading action. We establish exact refocusing for constant generators compatible with a two-segment echo, show that a four-frame Pauli cell cancels the leading contribution of any traceless quasi-static generator, and bound the residual error for smoothly varying birefringence. We then connect these guarantees to operational BB84 quantities, including measured QBERs, the resulting secret fraction, and insertion loss. In simulations of a 50 km fiber with spatially correlated birefringence, a representative design reduces the mean QBER from 6.11% to 0.224% at a device spacing of 1.25 km. With an assumed per-device transmission of t = 0.997, this raises the asymptotic key rate per launched pulse by a factor of approximately 2.5. For this parameter set, the best design in the tested scan is not the densest one: error suppression and optical loss create a finite operating window. These results provide a loss-aware design principle for passive polarization stabilization and suggest a low-overhead complement to active tracking in polarization-encoded QKD networks.

title: Quantum States With The Same Entanglement And Local Unitary Equivalence
authors: Julio I. de Vicente
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local operations assisted by classical communication (LOCC) play a fundamental role in the resource-theoretic formulation of entanglement theory inducing an operationally meaningful ordering in the set of entangled states. The particular class within LOCC of local unitary (LU) transformations is obviously closed under inversion. Thus, LU-equivalent states are interconvertible by LOCC and have therefore the same entanglement. For this reason LU-equivalence has been thoroughly studied in the context of entanglement theory. However, as I note here with a simple example, the converse is not true: there exist entangled states that are interconvertible by LOCC but which are not LU-equivalent. This motivates studying under which conditions LOCC interconvertibility is characterized by LU-equivalence. I provide a sufficient condition for this to hold. When one considers multipartite states with full entanglement dimensionality (as quantified by the Schmidt number vector) LOCC interconvertibility can only hold under LU-equivalence.

title: Weighted Quantum Signal Processing: Low-Depth Polynomial Approximation With Applications To Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
authors: Rohit Sarma Sarkar, Rupayan Bhattacharjee, Elias F. Combarro, Michele Grossi, Lirand\"e Pira, Carmen G. Almud\'ever, Sergi Abadal, Eduard Alarcon
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Signal Processing is a powerful quantum framework for generating and approximating univariate polynomials. However, QSP is often limited by circuit-depth bottlenecks and parity constraints on the class of realizable polynomials. In this work, we introduce Weighted Quantum Signal Processing, an extension of QSP in which a weight function is assigned to the central rotation operator. This formulation provides a deeper understanding of QSP, which emerges as the special case of WQSP with unit weights. The choice of weights determines the structure and expressive capabilities of WQSP circuits. When the weights are natural numbers greater than one, WQSP reduces to a pruned version of QSP, revealing parameter redundancies in the standard framework. Through appropriate selection of integer weights, WQSP achieves linear-to-exponential reductions in the number of parameters required to realize arbitrary bounded univariate polynomials while preserving approximation quality. For generic weights, we establish corresponding approximation error bounds and show that, in many cases, the approximation is exact. We analyze WQSP from both a deterministic perspective, where polynomial generation is formulated as the solution of a linear system, and a quantum machine learning perspective, where WQSP serves as a structured and expressive quantum learning model. We further employ this learning framework to parameterize learnable activation functions in Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks for multivariate function approximation. Our results show that WQSP provides a compact, flexible, and theoretically grounded framework for realizing arbitrary univariate polynomials while requiring significantly fewer trainable parameters than conventional QSP. This yields expressive and parameter-efficient neural architectures, highlighting the potential of WQSP as a scalable primitive for quantum-enhanced machine learning.
tldr: Introduces Weighted Quantum Signal Processing (WQSP), a generalization of QSP that assigns weights to the central rotation to reduce circuit depth and parameter count for polynomial approximation, with applications to Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks.
motivation: QSP is a powerful framework for polynomial approximation, but it suffers from circuit-depth bottlenecks and parity constraints that limit its efficiency and applicability to quantum machine learning.
method: WQSP assigns a weight function to the central rotation, enabling a deterministic linear-system formulation and a quantum machine learning perspective; integer weights prune QSP redundancies, and generic weights yield approximation error bounds.
result: Integer weights achieve linear-to-exponential reductions in the number of parameters needed to realize arbitrary bounded univariate polynomials while preserving approximation quality; WQSP also parameterizes learnable activation functions in Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks with fewer trainable parameters.
conclusion: WQSP provides a compact, flexible, and theoretically grounded framework for polynomial approximation and parameter-efficient quantum-enhanced machine learning.

title: Transcript-Bound Combiners For Downgrade-Resilient Hybrid Post-Quantum Key Establishment: Definition, Proof, And Embedded-Device Cost
authors: Sanjeev Rana Bhanwar Gupta
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hybrid key establishment runs a post-quantum key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) alongside a classical Diffie-Hellman primitive, so that the session key stays secure while either component resists attack. This design is now standardized in the Transport Layer Security protocol, Secure Shell, and the Internet Key Exchange, with the standardized module-lattice KEM (ML-KEM) as the post-quantum component. A hybrid KEM secures the derived key, but not the integrity of the negotiation that selects which primitives are used. Full protocols authenticate that negotiation through a handshake transcript; a hybrid KEM deployed as a standalone drop-in primitive, or inside a minimal handshake without transcript authentication, inherits no such guarantee, and an active attacker can strip the post-quantum option. We ask what the key schedule alone must contain to make downgrade resilience a local property of the combiner. We give a game-based definition at the combiner layer and prove a two-sided separation: a combiner that ignores the transcript is downgraded with certainty, whereas one that binds the session key and the confirmation tag to a hash of the transcript blocks every such attempt, up to a term negligible for a 256-bit transcript hash. We also give an explicit strongest-link security bound. Using a calibrated cost model composed from published Cortex-M4 measurements, transcript binding adds one hash per party - about 11.8% of handshake computation but only 1.5% of radio-inclusive energy - and adds no messages or bytes on the wire. Every reported number is produced by a released harness that passes a 30-check validation gate.
tldr: The paper defines transcript-bound combiners for hybrid post-quantum key establishment and proves downgrade resilience at the combiner layer, with embedded-device cost analysis.
motivation: Hybrid KEMs secure the derived key but not the integrity of the negotiation selecting primitives, so an active attacker can strip the post-quantum option when transcripts are unauthenticated.
method: It gives a game-based definition at the combiner layer and proves a two-sided separation, using a calibrated Cortex-M4 cost model and a released 30-check validation harness.
result: Transcript binding adds about 11.8% handshake computation and 1.5% radio-inclusive energy, with no extra messages or bytes on the wire and only negligible security loss for a 256-bit transcript hash.
conclusion: Binding the session key and confirmation tag to a transcript hash makes downgrade resilience a local property of the combiner, offering a practical security upgrade for embedded hybrid post-quantum deployments.

title: From Trainability Diagnostics To Optimization Claims: Boundaries And Controls In Variational Quantum Optimization
authors: Pilsung Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21243v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Barren plateau diagnostics characterize whether gradient signal remains available for training, but surviving signal need not translate into successful optimization. We study this trainability--optimization gap at the level of optimizer steps. Treating coefficient-weighted Hamiltonian-term gradients as task-like components, we introduce step-level diagnostics and derive an exact bridge between signed termwise organization, directional activity, and first-order descent. Resolving this bridge into standard first-order geometry shows that the apparent organization--activity factors are not independent optimization axes and that, at fixed state and update norm, the raw gradient maximizes first-order descent of the summed objective. We compare vanilla gradient descent, a deterministic Hamiltonian-term PCGrad variant, and probe-gated LSO-PCGrad on transverse-field Ising model instances with hardware-efficient and Hamiltonian variational ansatzes, together with matched controls for update norm and probe budget. Blind projection can improve an organization diagnostic while worsening final energy and first-order predictability. After conditioning on standard first-order geometry, residual term-space composition shows no reproducible material incremental association with realized descent, while optimizer-relative update norm shows positive material associations in some settings without cross-regime reproducibility. Matched controls provide no resolved final-energy benefit attributable to the projected direction, and the improvement of LSO-PCGrad is more consistent with probe-based search and step-norm adaptation than with Hamiltonian-term projection itself. These results show that gradient-structure diagnostics can characterize trainability and update geometry without serving as standalone evidence of optimization benefit, which requires controls matched on update norm and search budget.
tldr: The paper examines the gap between barren-plateau trainability diagnostics and actual optimization performance in variational quantum algorithms, showing gradient-structure diagnostics do not reliably predict optimization benefit.
motivation: Barren plateau diagnostics assess whether gradient signal remains available for training, but surviving signal may not translate into successful optimization; the study aims to clarify when trainability metrics can support optimization claims.
method: It introduces step-level diagnostics for coefficient-weighted Hamiltonian-term gradients, derives an exact bridge between signed termwise organization and first-order descent, and compares gradient descent, a PCGrad variant, and LSO-PCGrad on transverse-field Ising model instances with matched controls.
result: Blind projection can improve an organization diagnostic while worsening final energy and first-order predictability; after conditioning on first-order geometry, term-space composition shows no reproducible incremental association with realized descent, and LSO-PCGrad improvement appears driven by probe-based search and step-norm adaptation rather than projection.
conclusion: Gradient-structure diagnostics can characterize trainability and update geometry but require controls matched on update norm and search budget before serving as standalone evidence of optimization benefit.

title: Pauli-string Grouping For Vqe Measurement Reduction On A Sparse-connectivity Quantum Annealer
authors: Raul Martinez, Miguel Sanchez-Beato, Mario Calonge
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20861v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) requires a large number of measurements to evaluate molecular Hamiltonians. Expressing a molecular Hamiltonian as a linear combination of Pauli strings creates a measurement bottleneck: non-commuting Pauli strings cannot be measured simultaneously. Consequently, mutually commuting Pauli strings must be grouped and measured together to minimise the number of quantum-state preparations. This task maps to the minimum clique cover problem on a commutativity graph, an NP-hard problem typically addressed using classical heuristics. Although an Ising-model formulation has recently been explored on fully connected CMOS Ising machines and demonstrated on physical quantum annealers only at small scale, the embedding cost that governs its behaviour on hardware with sparse connectivity, where each logical variable must be represented by a chain of physical qubits, has not been characterised. In this work, we formulate the Pauli-grouping problem as a standard QUBO colouring model and study its scalability on a D-Wave quantum annealer. Across a series of molecular systems and for both qubit-wise and full commutativity, we quantify the growth in the number of logical variables and the QUBO interaction density, characterise the physical-qubit and chain-length overhead required for embedding on the Zephyr topology, and compare the annealer's time-to-solution and solution quality with those of heuristic classical baselines. This analysis identifies the threshold of molecular complexity beyond which hardware connectivity prevents viable embedding, and shows that a second, practical limit is reached earlier. The threshold therefore measures how far current annealers are from the regime in which pre-optimising a VQE measurement scheme on hardware would be worth considering.
tldr: The paper reformulates Pauli-string grouping for VQE measurement reduction as a QUBO colouring model and empirically characterizes its embedding overhead and scalability on a sparse-connectivity D-Wave quantum annealer.
motivation: VQE suffers from a measurement bottleneck because non-commuting Pauli strings cannot be measured jointly, and grouping them is an NP-hard minimum clique cover problem; recent quantum-annealer proposals have only been demonstrated at small scale without understanding embedding costs on sparse hardware.
method: The authors map Pauli grouping (both qubit-wise and full commutativity) to a standard QUBO colouring problem, quantify growth in logical variables and interaction density for several molecules, and characterize physical-qubit and chain-length overhead required to embed on the Zephyr topology, comparing annealer time-to-solution and solution quality against classical heuristics.
result: They identify a molecular-complexity threshold beyond which hardware connectivity prevents viable embedding, and find that a second, practical performance limit is reached even earlier, revealing how far current annealers are from being useful for pre-optimizing VQE measurement schemes.
conclusion: Quantum annealing for VQE measurement reduction is currently limited more by embedding overhead than by the underlying combinatorial problem, so hardware-based Pauli grouping is not yet competitive with classical heuristics.

title: Task-Oriented Quantization For Quadratic Scheduling: Centroid Water-Filling And Power-Diagram Encoders
authors: Joss Armstrong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We distinguish two regimes in task-oriented quantization with a known deterministic oracle action. For an unconstrained interior oracle and a smooth strongly concave utility, quantizing the oracle action by vector Lloyd-Max minimizes a mean-squared-error surrogate and achieves a [MATH] approximation to the optimal [MATH]-level task quantizer. The reduction is exact for isotropic quadratic loss, and the corresponding task rate--distortion function is bracketed by two ordinary rate--distortion functions. Budget-constrained quadratic scheduling is different: the oracle satisfies a variational inequality, so quantizing water-filled actions is not generally optimal. We derive the exact Lloyd-type conditions for this case. The optimal action for a quantizer cell is water-filling evaluated at the cell's conditional-mean load, and the optimal encoder partitions load space into affine power-diagram cells. Thus the correct prescription is to quantize the load and water-fill its centroid. The distinction is material whenever a cell crosses water-filling active-set boundaries.
tldr: This paper analyzes task-oriented quantization for quadratic scheduling, showing that for budget-constrained oracles one should quantize the load and water-fill its centroid rather than quantize water-filled actions.
motivation: Task-oriented quantization seeks to preserve downstream task performance, but optimal quantizer design for scheduling with deterministic oracle actions remains unclear, especially under budget constraints.
method: For unconstrained interior oracles, vector Lloyd-Max minimizes an MSE surrogate; for budget-constrained quadratic scheduling, the authors derive exact Lloyd-type conditions using conditional-mean load and affine power-diagram cells.
result: The optimal action is water-filling at the cell's conditional-mean load, and the correct encoder partitions load space into affine power-diagram cells; quantizing water-filled actions is not generally optimal.
conclusion: The distinction is material when cells cross water-filling active-set boundaries, clarifying task-oriented quantizer design for scheduling.

authors: Aditya Tyagi Nuh Aydin

Because [MATH] is not a field, the type of [MATH] ([MATH]) is not necessarily inherited by [MATH]. Determining conditions under which the type of [MATH] is inherited by [MATH] was posed as an open problem recently in . In this paper, we settle this problem. We first give two sufficient conditions for the type to be preserved: one requires a single [MATH] to be coprime to [MATH] over [MATH], the other only requires the [MATH] to be jointly coprime to it. Neither condition is necessary in general. motivation: Quasi-cyclic codes over Z_4 are constructed by picking a polynomial and forming a submodule, but since Z_4[x] is not a field, the type (structure) of the parent cyclic code is not automatically inherited, and the conditions for inheritance were posed as an open problem.
method: The authors give two sufficient conditions for type preservation, then exploit the fact that Z_4[x]/<x^m-1> is squarefree for odd m to decompose the ring into finite chain rings via the Chinese Remainder Theorem, deriving a necessary and sufficient condition based solely on irreducible factors where a certain polynomial does not vanish.

conclusion: The open problem on type inheritance for quasi-cyclic codes over Z_4 is settled, and the new criterion proves practically useful for constructing record-setting quaternary linear codes.

authors: Han Mao Kiah, Hengjia Wei, Ruixiao Zeng

We establish a combinatorial reduction that trades [MATH] units of insertion budget for one unit of deletion budget in the decoding guarantee, without changing the code or increasing the list size. Consequently, asymptotic bounds for mixed errors with insertion fraction [MATH] and deletion fraction [MATH] follow from insertion-only lower bounds at [MATH] and deletion-only upper bounds at [MATH]. For binary unique decoding, we strictly improve Levenshtein's classical asymptotic rate lower bound for every deletion fraction [MATH] for which the classical rate expression is nonnegative. At [MATH], the lower bound increases from approximately [MATH] to [MATH], a relative increase of about [MATH]. Our framework also yields insertion and deletion lower bounds for every fixed list size. The existence proofs combine the Lov\'asz local lemma with sampling from words having a specified number of runs, where a run is a maximal block of equal symbols. motivation: Insertion-deletion codes are fundamental in classical coding theory for adversarial error correction, but asymptotic rate bounds for list decoding and mixed errors remain incomplete.
method: The authors use a combinatorial reduction trading insertion budget for deletion budget, the Lovász local lemma with run-sampling, generating functions, and a higher-order Elias bound based on intersections and unions of position sets.
result: They strictly improve Levenshtein's lower bound for binary unique decoding at every deletion fraction, increase the rate at zero deletion fraction from approximately 0 to approximately 0.12, and improve Haeupler-Shahrasbi-Sudan insertion bounds for fixed list sizes.

title: Weighted Berry Curvature And Global Geometry Of Mixed Quantum States
authors: Erik Sj\"oqvist Dominik Kuczy\'nski
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21355v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examine the geometric interpretation of the quantum geometric tensor proposed in [Phys. Rev. B {\bf 110}, 035404 (2024)] for mixed quantum states, focusing on its imaginary part, which is proportional to a weighted sum of the Berry curvatures of the eigenstates of the density operator. While the real part naturally decomposes into Fisher--Rao and weighted Fubini--Study contributions, we show that the imaginary part does not, in general, coincide with the curvature of a connection on a globally defined U(1) line bundle whose holonomy yields a mixed-state geometric phase. Using a two-level system as an explicit example, we demonstrate that its surface integral depends on the choice of surface bounded by the same closed path, with ambiguities that are not integer multiples of [MATH].
tldr: The paper studies the imaginary part of a mixed-state quantum geometric tensor and shows it generally does not define a global U(1) connection, leading to surface-dependent mixed-state geometric phases.
motivation: Geometric phases and quantum geometric tensors are fundamental to understanding the geometry of quantum states, but their global bundle structure and surface independence for mixed states remain unclear.
method: The authors analyze a recently proposed quantum geometric tensor for mixed states, decompose its real part, and test the integrability of its imaginary part using an explicit two-level system.
result: The imaginary part is a weighted sum of eigenstate Berry curvatures, but its surface integral depends on the chosen surface bounded by the same closed path, with ambiguities not restricted to integer multiples of 2π.
conclusion: The mixed-state geometric phase derived from weighted Berry curvature is not globally well-defined as a U(1) holonomy, which affects geometric interpretations in mixed-state quantum information.

title: Critical And Near-critical Influence Bounds For Ferromagnetic Ising Models
authors: Yan Ru Pei

The estimate is uniform in the degree, the external fields, and all pinnings. More generally, if the couplings are bounded by [MATH] and [MATH], the bound is [MATH]. The proof combines a pointwise cavity bound with a positive-series magnetization tilt and the field comparison theorem of Ding, Song and Sun. The critical estimate removes the logarithm in recent general graphical bounds for the ferromagnetic case. As a consequence, zero-field single-site Glauber dynamics mixes in polynomial time throughout the supercritical window [MATH], with the polynomial degree depending on the window size.
tldr: The paper proves sharp influence bounds for ferromagnetic Ising models at and near criticality, implying polynomial-time mixing of Glauber dynamics in the supercritical window.
motivation: Influence decay in Ising models controls mixing times and phase transitions, but recent general graphical bounds contained an undesirable logarithmic factor for ferromagnetic systems.
method: The proof combines a pointwise cavity bound, a positive-series magnetization tilt, and the field comparison theorem of Ding, Song and Sun.
result: At the tree uniqueness threshold, every row of the influence matrix is bounded uniformly in degree, external fields, and pinnings, with a more general bound for bounded couplings; the critical estimate removes the logarithm.
conclusion: As a consequence, zero-field single-site Glauber dynamics mixes in polynomial time throughout the supercritical window, with the polynomial degree depending on the window size.

title: Bootstrapping Classical Systems With Quenched Disorder
authors: Minjae Cho, Yaprak \"onder, Eslam Khalaf, Michael G. Scheer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a bootstrap method for deriving bounds on disorder-averaged observables in classical statistical systems with quenched disorder. The three main ingredients of the bootstrap are the positivity of ensembles of probability measures, disorder-averaged equations of motion, and explicit expectation values of random coupling variables. Together, these ingredients lead to a linear programming problem over the space of disorder averages. By further employing the positivity of the two-replica Gram matrix, we also formulate a semidefinite programming problem that produces bounds on two-replica correlators. We demonstrate the method using two examples: the two-dimensional random site-diluted Ising model and the one-dimensional disordered contact process. For the latter example, the bootstrap bounds exhibit a region of multiple kinks that we relate to the Griffiths region, whose finite-size scaling analysis yields a typical correlation length exponent in good numerical agreement with the known value.
tldr: A bootstrap method is introduced for deriving bounds on disorder-averaged observables in classical statistical systems with quenched disorder, demonstrated on random Ising and disordered contact process models.
motivation: Disordered classical systems are challenging to analyze nonperturbatively due to averaging and rare-region effects, motivating new rigorous bounding techniques.
method: The approach combines positivity of probability measures, disorder-averaged equations of motion, and explicit random-coupling expectations into linear and semidefinite programs over disorder averages and two-replica correlators.
result: Applied to the two-dimensional random site-diluted Ising model and the one-dimensional disordered contact process, the latter yielding bounds with kinks associated with the Griffiths region and a typical correlation length exponent matching known values.
conclusion: The bootstrap provides a novel computational tool for classical disordered systems and can capture Griffiths-phase physics, though it lies outside quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems.

title: Hybrid Quantum-classical Attention For Histopathology-based Molecular Profiling In Data-limited Cancers
authors: Kahn Rhrissorrakrai, Aritra Bose, Aldo Guzman-Saenz, Filippo Utro, Laxmi Pardia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Molecular profiling from routine histopathology could expand access to precision oncology when sequencing is unavailable, tissue is limited, or training cohorts are small. We developed a hybrid quantum-classical strategy that replaces softmax attention in a transformer for histopathology-based gene expression prediction with a quantum-derived doubly stochastic matrix (QDSM). Across 29 cancer cohorts from The Cancer Genome Atlas and an independent pancreatic cancer cohort from the Clinical Proteomic Tumor Analysis Consortium, QDSM attention produced selective gains, with the largest relative improvements in smaller, data-limited cohorts, including adrenocortical carcinoma and uveal melanoma. Rather than improving transcriptome-wide performance uniformly, QDSM redistributed predictive accuracy across genes and pathways, improving biologically relevant targets in some tumor contexts while worsening others. In adrenocortical carcinoma, preferentially improved genes were enriched for adverse overall-survival associations, linking enhanced molecular inference to prognostically relevant biology. In pancreatic cancer transfer experiments, QDSM improved selected metabolic and lineage-associated genes but did not consistently improve performance under cross-cohort shift. Leave-one-cancer-out mixed-effects analysis showed that baseline molecular features predicted part of the gene-level benefit, while residuals identified cancer-specific programs that improved more or less than expected. Separate experiments on IBM quantum processors recovered the doubly stochastic matrix primitive underlying the attention mechanism. These findings position QDSM attention as a context- and target-dependent strategy for image-based molecular profiling and molecular triage when direct testing is unavailable, incomplete, or impractical.
tldr: The paper introduces a hybrid quantum-classical attention mechanism using a quantum-derived doubly stochastic matrix (QDSM) for histopathology-based gene expression prediction in data-limited cancers.
motivation: Molecular profiling from routine histopathology could improve precision oncology when sequencing is unavailable, tissue is limited, or training cohorts are small, but standard attention may not perform well in these settings.
method: The authors replace softmax attention in a transformer with a QDSM, evaluated across 29 TCGA cancer cohorts and a CPTAC pancreatic cohort, with validation on IBM quantum processors.
result: QDSM attention produced selective, context-dependent gains, largest in smaller cohorts like adrenocortical carcinoma and uveal melanoma, but did not uniformly improve performance across genes or under cross-cohort shift.
conclusion: QDSM attention is a context- and target-dependent strategy for image-based molecular profiling and molecular triage, though benefits vary by cancer type and transfer setting.

title: Persistence, Resetting, And First-passage Times Of An Active Ornstein--Uhlenbeck Particle
authors: Demosthenes K. Georgiou, Paul C. Bressloff, Thibault Bertrand
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the first-passage time statistics of an active Ornstein--Uhlenbeck particle on a finite one-dimensional interval with an absorbing boundary at one end and a reflecting boundary at the other, subject to stochastic resetting. In the weak-activity regime, we develop a perturbative solution of the Fokker--Planck equation and use a renewal framework to obtain analytical expressions for the first-passage-time distribution and its low-order moments. In the absence of resetting, activity can either increase or decrease the mean first-passage time, depending on the relation between the persistence time and the diffusive time to absorption. When resetting is introduced, we determine both the onset of beneficial resetting and the finite range of resetting rates for which resetting lowers the mean first-passage time of the active system. We further show that the resetting transition depends on the velocity resetting protocol. Finally, by comparing the active particle with resetting to the passive Brownian particle without resetting, we construct a phase diagram that identifies the regions of parameter space in which activity and resetting together reduce the mean first-passage time.
tldr: A perturbative Fokker-Planck and renewal-theory study of first-passage time statistics for an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle on a finite interval under stochastic resetting.
motivation: Active particles exhibit persistent motion that qualitatively alters escape and search kinetics, and stochastic resetting is known to optimize first-passage times; understanding how activity and resetting combine is an open question in nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.
method: The authors develop a weak-activity perturbative solution of the Fokker-Planck equation for an active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle with absorbing/reflecting boundaries, and use a renewal framework to derive analytical expressions for the first-passage-time distribution and its low-order moments, including under velocity-dependent resetting protocols.
result: Activity can either increase or decrease the mean first-passage time depending on the ratio of persistence time to diffusive absorption time; with resetting they identify an onset and a finite window of beneficial resetting rates, show the resetting transition depends on the velocity resetting protocol, and construct a phase diagram delimiting where activity plus resetting reduces the mean first-passage time relative to passive Brownian motion.
conclusion: The work clarifies how persistence and resetting jointly govern absorption kinetics of active particles, providing a phase-diagram classification of parameter regimes where activity and resetting cooperatively accelerate first passage.

title: A Functorial Theory Of Defects In Abelian Chern-Simons Theory
authors: Daniel Galviz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work has constructed Abelian Chern-Simons theories as categorical TQFTs, allowing us to naturally incorporate categorical defects and construct defect extensions of Abelian Chern-Simons TQFTs. We first identify the Turaev-Viro realizations of Abelian Chern-Simons theory in the center and doubled pointed modular cases, clarifying the distinction between single bulk realizations and canonical doubled ones. Alternatively, the Alterfold construction supplies the associated topological boundaries, domain walls, and condensation sectors, establishing an explicit Alterfold/Chern-Simons dictionary. We show that the finite quadratic module is the invariant controlling the bulk theory, its topological symmetries, orientation-reversal invariance, and defects. We further show that multicomponent Abelian BF theory arises as the extended TQFT of an off-diagonal Abelian Chern-Simons theory, placing it naturally within the same extended framework. Finally, we demonstrate that recently proposed Abelian Chern-Simons dualities do not define a genuine TQFT duality. These results provide a concrete model for defects in Abelian topological orders and suggest a route toward the non-Abelian case.
tldr: The paper develops a functorial theory of defects in Abelian Chern-Simons theory using categorical TQFT, Alterfold, and finite quadratic modules.
motivation: Recent work constructed Abelian Chern-Simons theories as categorical TQFTs, enabling the incorporation of categorical defects and defect extensions.
method: The author uses Turaev-Viro realizations, the Alterfold construction, and finite quadratic modules to analyze bulk theory, symmetries, boundaries, and defects.
result: It identifies Turaev-Viro realizations, establishes an Alterfold/Chern-Simons dictionary, shows multicomponent Abelian BF theory arises as an extended TQFT, and argues that proposed Abelian Chern-Simons dualities are not genuine TQFT dualities.
conclusion: The results provide a concrete model for defects in Abelian topological orders and suggest a route toward the non-Abelian case.

title: Topological Characterization Of A Reconfigurable Synthetic-frequency Ssh Lattice On An Integrated Lithium-niobate Platform
authors: Hiep Xuan Dinh, Armandas Bal\v{c}ytis, Guanghui Ren, Mei Xian Low, Arnan Mitchell, Thach G. Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21440v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthetic frequency dimensions provide a powerful and highly reconfigurable platform for topological photonics. However, experimentally identifying their topological phases remains challenging because these systems do not naturally provide well-defined boundaries or readily accessible edge-state signatures. Here, we realize a reconfigurable Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) lattice in a synthetic frequency dimension using an integrated thin-film lithium-niobate photonic molecule and directly measure its topology. Electro-optic coupling between staggered resonator supermodes enables independent control of the effective intra-cell and inter-cell hopping strengths, enabling dynamic switching between trivial and non-trivial topological phases on the same chip. We validate the transition through two independently derived bulk topological invariants: direct retrieval of Zak phase from time-resolved synthetic-dimension band-structure spectroscopy; and extraction of the winding number using mean-chiral-displacement method from site-resolved steady-state measurements. Both approaches consistently identify the topological transition and agree closely with theoretical predictions. Our results demonstrate experimentally accessible, boundary-independent methods for characterizing topology in synthetic-frequency lattices. More broadly, the integrated and dynamically reconfigurable photonic platform provides a scalable framework for bulk topological characterization and programmable topological photonic systems.
tldr: The paper realizes a reconfigurable Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice in a synthetic frequency dimension on an integrated lithium niobate platform and measures its topological invariants.
motivation: Synthetic frequency dimensions offer a reconfigurable platform for topological photonics, but experimentally identifying topological phases is challenging because such systems lack well-defined boundaries or readily accessible edge-state signatures.
method: They use an electro-optic photonic molecule with staggered resonator supermodes to independently control effective intra-cell and inter-cell hopping strengths, and retrieve bulk topological invariants via time-resolved synthetic-dimension band-structure spectroscopy (Zak phase) and site-resolved steady-state measurements (winding number).
result: They demonstrate dynamic switching between trivial and non-trivial topological phases on the same chip, with both the Zak phase and winding number consistently identifying the topological transition and agreeing closely with theoretical predictions.
conclusion: The work provides experimentally accessible, boundary-independent methods for characterizing topology in synthetic-frequency lattices and offers a scalable integrated platform for programmable topological photonic systems.

title: Lidskii Theorem For Directional Derivatives Of Symplectic Eigenvalues
authors: Hemant K. Mishra
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21620v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present a refinement of the symplectic Lidskii theorem for directional derivatives of symplectic eigenvalues, which is inspired by the work of Sendov [Electron. J. Linear Algebra 41(2025), 338-341]. We show that for a [MATH] real positive definite matrix [MATH] and symmetric matrices [MATH] d'(A;H+K)-d'(A;H) \prec_{\pi_A} d'(A;K). Here [MATH] represents block-majorization corresponding to the partition [MATH] of [MATH] given by the equality blocks of symplectic eigenvalues of [MATH]. We know that Hermitianization of a symmetric matrix occurs in the directional derivative expression of symplectic eigenvalues. We establish a componentwise inequality comparing the symplectic eigenvalues of a positive definite matrix with the ordinary eigenvalues of its associated Hermitianization, and also characterize the equality case. By using the aforementioned inequality, we then show that the symplectic Lidskii theorem follows from the directional derivative Lidskii theorem.

motivation: Inspired by recent work of Sendov, the author aims to extend Lidskii-type theorems to the symplectic eigenvalue setting, which is a purely linear-algebraic problem with potential connections to matrix analysis.
method: The approach establishes a componentwise inequality comparing symplectic eigenvalues of a positive definite matrix with the ordinary eigenvalues of its Hermitianization, and then uses this inequality to derive the directional derivative Lidskii theorem.
result: The main result is a refinement of the symplectic Lidskii theorem: for a real positive definite matrix A and symmetric matrices H, K, the difference of directional derivatives satisfies a block-majorization relation corresponding to the equality blocks of symplectic eigenvalues of A.
