title: Set-Packing And Sequence-Pair QUBOs For The 2d Cutting Stock Problem On Quantum Annealing Hardware
authors: Miguel S\'anchez-Beato, Raul Martinez, Matilde Osa, Jorge Parra, Mario Calonge
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20853v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The two-dimensional Cutting Stock Problem (2D-CSP) is an NP-hard problem with direct economic and environmental impacts on manufacturing and logistics. We encode its fixed-plate variant, with free piece repetition and full non-overlap and containment constraints, as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem for quantum annealing and compare two formulations from opposite encoding paradigms. The first was a coordinate-based set-packing model with one binary variable per candidate placement. Its variable count grows linearly with plate area and resolution, but its ground state is, by construction, a geometrically feasible maximum-area packing. The second is a coordinate-free sequence-pair model whose variable count is independent of plate resolution and size. We prove that this compactness has a structural limit: no coordinate-free QUBO of bounded interaction degree whose penalties vanish on every geometrically feasible layout can have a geometrically feasible ground state for 2D containment, because containment is a longest-path constraint that bounded-degree penalties cannot enforce on chains longer than their interaction order. We evaluate both formulations under multi-seed simulated annealing, simulated quantum annealing, and an exact integer-programming baseline. Hardware experiments include D-Wave minor embedding, a calibrated direct-QPU sweep, and Leap hybrid solvers in both penalty and constraint-native form, across a six-instance campaign with per-instance calibration. The hybrid solver returns our certificate configuration, tying its energy to thirteen decimal places while overflowing the plate. We claim no quantum speedup. Our contribution is an impossibility result characterizing the limits of compact packing QUBOs, and a practical rule for choosing between the two formulations.
tldr: The paper formulates the two-dimensional cutting stock problem as QUBO for quantum annealing, compares two encodings, and proves an impossibility result for compact coordinate-free QUBOs.
motivation: The 2D cutting stock problem is NP-hard with industrial impact, and quantum annealing is explored as an optimization platform for QUBO formulations.
method: The authors propose a coordinate-based set-packing QUBO and a coordinate-free sequence-pair QUBO, then benchmark them via simulated annealing, simulated quantum annealing, exact integer programming, and D-Wave hardware experiments.
result: The sequence-pair QUBO has a structural limit: no bounded-degree coordinate-free QUBO can enforce 2D containment for arbitrarily long chains, and hardware/hybrid solvers return infeasible configurations despite matching energies.
conclusion: The work provides an impossibility result on compact packing QUBOs and a practical rule for choosing between formulations, but claims no quantum speedup.

title: Functional Renormalization For Random Matrix Theory: The Relational Background Field Method
authors: Dine Ousmane Samary Vincent Lahoche
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21031v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The construction of a reliable renormalization group (RG) flow for discrete gravity models that preserves their underlying symmetry group, typically [MATH] or [MATH], remains an open problem. For random matrix models, which are the focus of this paper, this symmetry is intrinsically tied to the interactions encoding the random geometry of two-dimensional quantum Euclidean spacetime. We develop a novel approach based on the introduction of a partial matrix-valued intermediate field. In the large-[MATH] limit, measure concentration strongly suppresses fluctuations of its singular values, allowing it to play the role of a self-consistent background field. This provides the basis for a relational RG in which the notion of scale is dynamically induced by the effective Gaussian measure in the basis where the intermediate field is diagonal. Our construction preserves the symmetry of the original model and admits a well-defined continuum limit. We show that the resulting infrared theory is described by a three-dimensional non-local Euclidean field theory with a non-trivial Wilson-Fisher-like fixed point and a single relevant direction. Remarkably, the associated critical exponent exactly matches the standard double-scaling exponent. We finally discuss extensions of the background-field approach to other discrete gravity models, such as random tensor models, and to different symmetry groups, as well as connections with more formal RG frameworks and information geometry.
tldr: The paper develops a relational functional renormalization group approach for random matrix models of 2D discrete quantum gravity using a matrix-valued intermediate background field.
motivation: Constructing a reliable renormalization group flow for discrete gravity models that preserves their underlying symmetry group remains an open problem, especially for random matrix models tied to random geometry.
method: The authors introduce a partial matrix-valued intermediate field whose singular-value fluctuations are suppressed in the large-N limit, allowing it to act as a self-consistent background and induce a dynamical scale via the effective Gaussian measure.
result: The resulting infrared theory is a three-dimensional non-local Euclidean field theory with a non-trivial Wilson-Fisher-like fixed point and a single relevant direction, and its critical exponent matches the standard double-scaling exponent.
conclusion: The construction preserves the original symmetry and admits a continuum limit, with possible extensions to random tensor models, other symmetry groups, formal RG frameworks, and information geometry.

title: Shock-Capturing Quantum Algorithm For The Linear Advection Operator
authors: Samuel Hagele, William Gregory, Yuan Shi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21153v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The linear advection operator is an ubiquitous building block in fluid and plasma problems. We develop a quantum algorithm for enacting the operator. When the advection velocity is constant in space, our algorithm is exponentially more efficient per time step than classical and avoids spurious oscillations near steep gradients. The algorithm is most cleanly illustrated using the one-dimensional advection equation on a uniform spatial grid with periodic boundary conditions, which can be extended to higher dimensions. The algorithm uses a first-order upwind scheme, which captures discontinuities in the wave envelope but is not unitary. We embed the non-unitary upwind scheme using Linear Combinations of Unitaries (LCUs), and develop an efficient quantum gate decomposition of the upwind unitary, which performs one step of advection using [MATH] two-qubit gates, where [MATH] is the number of spatial grid points, as opposed to a classical computer which costs [MATH]. Although LCUs introduces a small bounded probability of failure per time step, we show that the accumulation of failures does not lead to exponential-in-time complexity as one would naively expect. Moreover, when LCUs fails, we develop a probabilistic scheme to recover from the failure state, which avoids a full restart of the simulation. The failure recovery scheme uses quantum Fourier transform (QFT) and effectively achieves quantum indefinite integration of an unknown quantum state. The recovery, which can itself fail, is more efficient than a full restart if the wave envelop is well-resolved to include only low Fourier modes. We emulate our scheme classically and demonstrate small problems on Quantinuum's trapped-ion qubits. Our quantum algorithm provides a subroutine for physics simulations that involve linear advection.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for the linear advection operator using LCUs and QFT-based failure recovery, demonstrated on trapped-ion qubits.
motivation: The linear advection operator is ubiquitous in fluid and plasma simulations, motivating efficient quantum algorithms for this building block.
method: The non-unitary first-order upwind scheme is embedded via Linear Combinations of Unitaries (LCUs), with an efficient gate decomposition and a probabilistic QFT-based recovery scheme for LCU failures.
result: The algorithm is exponentially more efficient per time step than classical methods, avoids spurious oscillations near steep gradients, and maintains bounded failure accumulation without exponential time complexity.
conclusion: This provides a quantum subroutine for physics simulations involving linear advection, with potential extensions to higher dimensions.

title: On The Fourier Entropy-Influence Conjecture For Boolean Plateaued Functions
authors: Vladimir N. Potapov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21563v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the following inequality for Boolean functions: [MATH]. Using this inequality, we establish the Fourier Entropy-Influence (FEI) conjecture for Boolean plateaued functions. In particular, we show that the sharp FEI constant for the class of plateaued functions is 4. We also prove the FEI conjecture for partially bent functions and show that the corresponding sharp constant is 2. Finally, we derive several estimates for the p-biased distribution on the Boolean hypercube. Keywords: Fourier entropy, total influence, average sensitivity, plateaued function, algebraic degree, Reed-Muller code, p-biased distribution.
tldr: The paper proves an inequality for Boolean functions and uses it to establish the Fourier Entropy-Influence conjecture for plateaued and partially bent functions, determining sharp constants.
motivation: The Fourier Entropy-Influence conjecture is a longstanding open problem in the analysis of Boolean functions, relating Fourier entropy to total influence, with implications in learning theory and complexity.
method: The author derives a general inequality involving Fourier coefficients and influence, then specializes it to plateaued and partially bent functions, and analyzes the p-biased distribution on the Boolean hypercube.
result: The FEI conjecture holds for Boolean plateaued functions with sharp constant 4, and for partially bent functions with sharp constant 2; additional estimates for p-biased distributions are obtained.
conclusion: These results resolve the FEI conjecture for important subclasses of Boolean functions and provide sharp constants, while the general conjecture remains open.

title: Metasurface-integrated Vcsel Designed For Polarization Control In Optical Ising Machines
authors: Wenjie Chen, Zifeng Yuan, Hong-Lin Lin, Luo Qi, Jiaru Chu, Aaron Danner, Yuhang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The orthogonal polarization states of vertical-cavity surface-emitting lasers (VCSELs) can be used to describe candidate solutions to the Ising Hamiltonian, which is useful for solving quadratic unconstrained binary optimization problems. However, the natural anisotropy of VCSELs tends to overly favor one polarization state, which impedes the system from working as desired. In this work, we have designed and fabricated a metasurface, which may lead to a VCSEL with reduced undesired anisotropy. By changing the geometric size of nano-structures in the metasurface, the polarization state of the output light can be altered. Based on the injection-locking theory and spin-flip model, we numerically show that VCSELs with lowered anisotropy are more easily affected by the injection locking needed in Ising systems. Additionally, we numerically study the evolution of a 3-bit VCSEL-based Ising system and verify that the computational accuracy of the photonic Ising machine can be improved to more than twice that of its counterpart with higher anisotropy.
tldr: The paper designs a metasurface-integrated VCSEL to reduce polarization anisotropy for improved performance in optical Ising machines.
motivation: VCSELs can represent Ising spins via orthogonal polarization states, but natural anisotropy biases one polarization and degrades optimization accuracy.
method: A metasurface with tunable nano-structures is fabricated to control output polarization; injection-locking theory and the spin-flip model are used to simulate VCSEL dynamics and a 3-bit Ising system.
result: Lowered anisotropy makes VCSELs more susceptible to injection locking, and the 3-bit Ising machine achieves more than twice the computational accuracy of a higher-anisotropy counterpart.
conclusion: Metasurface engineering of VCSEL polarization anisotropy offers a route to more accurate photonic Ising machines for quadratic unconstrained binary optimization.

title: Physics-aware Hyper-reduction For Full-vector Photonic Waveguide Mode Solvers
authors: Lorena Vel\'azquez-Ibarra Daniel Rodr\'iguez-Guill\'en
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20948v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Photonic waveguide design often requires repeated full-vector Maxwell eigenmode solves over wavelength and geometry, where the subpixel smoothing needed at dielectric interfaces makes operator assembly a substantial part of the cost. We present a physics-aware hyper-reduction framework for accelerating this assembly. The method exploits an exact affine dependence of the discrete operators on the locally sampled inverse-permittivity tensor, and chooses its strategy from how a parameter acts on the interface cells. We demonstrate two regimes. In wavelength sweeps at fixed geometry, tensor values change on a fixed set of cells, and proper orthogonal decomposition with matrix discrete empirical interpolation reproduces the operators from few snapshots. In moving-boundary sweeps, interface information relocates across the grid, and event-driven dynamic local sampling updates only the coefficients a geometric step changes, reproducing full assembly exactly. These results show that operator assembly can be reduced by more than an order of magnitude without approximating the moving boundary, shifting the cost of a photonic mode sweep to the eigensolver.
tldr: The paper presents a physics-aware hyper-reduction framework that accelerates operator assembly in full-vector photonic waveguide eigenmode solvers by exploiting affine dependence of discrete operators on locally sampled inverse-permittivity tensors.
motivation: Photonic waveguide design requires repeated full-vector Maxwell eigenmode solves across wavelength and geometry, and subpixel smoothing at dielectric interfaces makes operator assembly a dominant cost.
method: The authors use proper orthogonal decomposition with matrix discrete empirical interpolation (POD-MDEIM) for wavelength sweeps with fixed interface cells, and an event-driven dynamic local sampling scheme for moving-boundary sweeps that updates only coefficients changed by each geometric step.
result: Both regimes reproduce full operator assembly with high fidelity, reducing assembly cost by more than an order of magnitude and shifting the computational bottleneck to the eigensolver.
conclusion: Physics-aware hyper-reduction enables substantial speedups in photonic mode sweeps without approximating moving boundaries, offering a practical numerical tool for waveguide design workflows.

title: Arctic Curves And A Gapped Gas Phase In A Two-Band Free-Fermion Chain
authors: Charles Jordan, Dimitri M. Gangardt, Alexander G. Abanov
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21004v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the imaginary-time evolution of a domain-wall state constrained to return to itself in a staggered free-fermion chain. The resulting space-time profile separates into frozen, liquid, and gas phases divided by sharp boundaries known as arctic curves. The spectral gap produces an incompressible half-filled gas phase bounded by an inner arctic curve, in addition to the outer frozen-liquid boundary. We determine both arctic curves, the thermodynamic return amplitude, and the complete equal-time correlation kernel. Correlations decay algebraically in the liquid regions and exponentially in the gas, while both arctic boundaries arise as caustics of free quasiparticle trajectories. The return amplitude and correlation kernel are respectively controlled by the determinant and inverse of the same block-Toeplitz operator. We obtain an exact matrix Wiener-Hopf factorization of this operator by reducing the problem to a scalar Riemann-Hilbert problem on an elliptic spectral curve. The factorization also yields the exact thermodynamic return amplitude: its logarithm consists of a quadratic term with explicit gap dependence and a bounded periodic theta-function correction. The resulting frozen-liquid-gas structure is a continuous-time free-fermion counterpart of that found in doubly periodic dimer models.
tldr: The paper analyzes imaginary-time evolution of a domain-wall state in a staggered free-fermion chain, deriving arctic curves and an incompressible half-filled gas phase via exact Wiener-Hopf factorization.
motivation: The authors aim to understand non-equilibrium space-time profiles and correlation structure in constrained free-fermion dynamics, extending arctic-curve phenomena from dimer models to a continuous-time quantum chain.
method: They use free-fermion techniques, block-Toeplitz determinants, matrix Wiener-Hopf factorization, and reduction to a scalar Riemann-Hilbert problem on an elliptic spectral curve.
result: They obtain both arctic curves, the thermodynamic return amplitude, and the complete equal-time correlation kernel, showing algebraic decay in liquid regions, exponential decay in the gas phase, and an exact return amplitude with quadratic gap dependence plus periodic theta-function corrections.
conclusion: The frozen-liquid-gas structure is a continuous-time free-fermion counterpart of doubly periodic dimer models, highlighting the role of spectral gaps in generating an inner arctic boundary.

title: Fundamental Bounds On The Polarizability Of Macroscopic Scatterers
authors: Miloslav Capek Lukas Jelinek
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Polarizability predicts how an object responds to an incident electromagnetic field, the interactions between small particles, or the optical forces exerted upon them. Polarizability is responsible for the effective-medium properties of artificial materials or metasurfaces. Despite significant progress in all these areas, it is unclear what the limits of the strength of such interactions are or, more specifically, what the upper bounds on the polarizability of a given spatial region that an unknown and designed particle would occupy are. This work connects the electromagnetic field description via an integral equation with a dual formulation of quadratic programming to derive fundamental bounds on components of all four polarizability tensors or on their specific combinations. In particular, the work establishes an intuitive visualization of what strong polarizability means and how strong it can be. The developed fundamental bound also answers which materials and domains are best for the given demands on polarizability. These findings establish a versatile platform that can accommodate a wide range of demands on polarizable bodies, providing an absolute measure of their performance against which the results of human-powered or automated design procedures can be compared.
tldr: The paper derives fundamental upper bounds on the polarizability tensors of macroscopic scatterers by connecting electromagnetic integral equations with dual quadratic programming.
motivation: Polarizability governs electromagnetic interactions, effective-medium properties, and optical forces, but the absolute limits on how strongly a designed particle of a given spatial region can respond were unclear.
method: The electromagnetic field description via an integral equation is combined with a dual formulation of quadratic programming to bound components of all four polarizability tensors and their combinations.
result: The work provides an intuitive visualization of strong polarizability, identifies best materials and domains for given demands, and establishes absolute performance benchmarks for human or automated design.
conclusion: These fundamental bounds offer a versatile platform for comparing and guiding the design of polarizable bodies, though the results are classical-electromagnetic and not quantum-information-theoretic.

title: Pair Density Shannon Information Measures And Their $N$-dependent Behaviour In Diatomic Molecular Systems
authors: Saul J. C. Salazar, J. Antonio Zarate, J. M. Solano-Altamirano, Humberto G. Laguna, Julio M. Hernandez-Perez, Robin P. Sagar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21260v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pair density Shannon entropies and mutual information in position and in momentum space are calculated for two series of homonuclear and heteronuclear diatomic molecules using Hartree-Fock wave functions. The pair density entropy sum increases with the quality of the basis set. Mutual information, a measure of statistical correlation, is seen to be smaller in momentum space as compared to position space. The interpretation is that the momentum pair density is closer than the position pair density to a Hartree-like reference. The [MATH]-dependent behaviours of the entropy and mutual information sums are examined by fitting the data to three different model behaviours. Results show that these models are capable of representing the molecular data in differing degrees. The parameters obtained from a particular model are relatively constant across different chemical series. This adds evidence to the argument of a universal [MATH]-dependent behaviour of the entropy sums.
tldr: The paper computes Shannon entropies and mutual information of pair densities for diatomic molecules using Hartree-Fock wave functions and analyzes their N-dependent behavior.
motivation: To understand statistical correlation and information content in molecular pair densities, and to test universal N-dependent scaling laws for entropy sums in position and momentum space.
method: Pair density Shannon entropies and mutual information are calculated from Hartree-Fock wave functions for homonuclear and heteronuclear diatomic molecules, and fitted to three model N-dependent behaviors.
result: The entropy sum increases with basis set quality, mutual information is smaller in momentum space than position space, and model parameters are relatively constant across chemical series, supporting universal N-dependent behavior.
conclusion: The study provides evidence for universal N-dependent scaling of Shannon information measures in diatomic molecules, with momentum pair densities closer to a Hartree-like reference than position pair densities.

title: Mechanical Activation Of Terahertz Tunneling In Metallic Nanogaps
authors: Dasom Kim, Dukhyung Lee, Young-Mi Bahk, Dai-Sik Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21506v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metallic nanogaps concentrate terahertz (THz) fields into deep subwavelength volumes and support field-driven electron tunneling when the insulating barrier becomes sufficiently narrow. Here, we demonstrate mechanical control of tunneling-mediated nonlinear THz transmission in a flexible nanogap metasurface. The metasurface consists of Au/PMMA/Au nanogaps fabricated on a polyethylene terephthalate substrate, enabling continuous tuning of the gap geometry through macroscopic bending. In the flat state, the resonant transmission exhibits only a weak dependence on the incident THz field strength. Upon bending, increasing the incident field strength induces pronounced resonance suppression accompanied by saturation of the voltage developed across the nanogaps. This nonlinear response is consistent with the opening of a field-dependent tunneling conduction channel through the mechanically narrowed PMMA barriers. Simmons-model calculations illustrate the strong increase in tunneling current density and the associated dissipative gap response as the local gap width approaches the few-nanometer regime. These results establish mechanical deformation as a macroscopic means of controlling tunneling-mediated THz nonlinearities in flexible metasurfaces.
tldr: Mechanical bending of a flexible Au/PMMA/Au nanogap metasurface tunes terahertz-field-driven electron tunneling, producing nonlinear resonance suppression.
motivation: Metallic nanogaps concentrate THz fields to deep subwavelength volumes and can host field-driven tunneling, but dynamic, macroscopic control of this tunneling-mediated nonlinearity has not been demonstrated.
method: Au/PMMA/Au nanogaps were fabricated on a flexible polyethylene terephthalate substrate, and macroscopic bending was used to continuously tune the gap geometry while measuring field-dependent nonlinear THz transmission; Simmons-model calculations were used to interpret the tunneling current.
result: In the flat state the nonlinear response is weak, whereas bending narrows the PMMA barriers and, with increasing THz field strength, causes pronounced resonance suppression and saturation of the gap voltage, consistent with a field-dependent tunneling channel.
conclusion: Mechanical deformation provides a macroscopic knob for controlling tunneling-mediated THz nonlinearities in flexible metasurfaces, offering a route to tunable THz devices.

title: An $m^{2.943}$ Bohnenblust--Hille Bound On The Boolean Cube
authors: Joseph Slote, Chun-Kai Tseng, Alexander Volberg
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let [MATH] and put \[ \beta_0={2}+{\log 2}=2.9426950408\ldots, \] where [MATH] is the natural logarithm. title: The Refutation Gap: Certifying Both Halves Of An Optimality Claim
authors: Rohan Pandey
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthesis pipelines increasingly claim not just that a program is correct, but that it is optimal. Such a claim has two halves with radically different verification stories. The upper bound, "a program of size m exists", is witnessed by an artifact that can be re-executed, proved equivalent to its specification, and shipped with a machine-checked certificate. The lower bound, "no program of size m-1 exists", has no witness and is discharged by running a solver until it reports UNSAT. Combinatorial optimization has known this asymmetry for decades and has largely addressed it: certifying algorithms make it explicit (McConnell et al., 2011), and pseudo-Boolean proof logging can certify optimality end to end with a formally verified checker (Bogaerts et al., 2023; Koops et al., 2025). That discipline has not reached circuit minimization. We call this the refutation gap: published gate counts for minimal XOR circuits provide no certificate for either half of the claim, and neither did 121 optimality results we ourselves produced. We close the gap with a pipeline that synthesizes minimal linear straight-line programs over GF(2), where every decisive UNSAT answer emits a DRAT proof checked by an independent third-party checker. We certify all 121 optimality results established by the project, across n = 6 to 9: 111 carry independently verified refutations, 10 are closed by a free counting bound, and none disagrees with the uncertified value. The median proof is 1.1 MB and checking costs 1.9x solving. We give five case studies where verification caught defects that code review did not, report two interface obstacles that push practitioners toward the uncertified path, and describe an adversarial audit that revealed a failure tail we were about to attribute to the problem was actually caused by our own budget.
tldr: The paper identifies a 'refutation gap' in optimality claims for circuit minimization and closes it by coupling a minimal GF(2) linear-program synthesizer with DRAT proof logging to certify UNSAT lower bounds.
motivation: Synthesis pipelines routinely assert optimality, but the lower-bound half ('no smaller program exists') admits no witness and is normally just a solver's UNSAT verdict, leaving published gate counts unverifiable.
method: The authors build a pipeline that synthesizes minimal linear straight-line programs over GF(2) and emits a DRAT proof for every decisive UNSAT answer, checked by an independent third-party verifier; they also report interface obstacles and an adversarial audit.
result: All 121 optimality results (n = 6 to 9) are certified — 111 with independently verified refutations and 10 via a counting bound — with none disagreeing with uncertified values; median proofs are 1.1 MB and checking costs 1.9x solving.
conclusion: Formally checkable refutations can be integrated into classical circuit-minimization workflows, catching defects code review misses, though practical obstacles still push practitioners toward uncertified paths.

title: Phase-Flow Topology Of Bound States In The Continuum
authors: Nikolai A. Vlasov, Varvara P. Panurchenko, Ravshanjon Kh. Nazarov, Stanislav S. Baturin, Ekaterina E. Maslova, Zarina F. Kondratenko
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20956v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Control of topological charges of bound states in the continuum (BICs) is essential for advanced topological photonics. A rigorous theoretical framework for understanding the formation of these charges is therefore necessary for further progress in this field. However, conventional multipolar formalism often fail to predict the topological charge when no single multipole dominates the mode. To address this fundamental issue, we present a rigorous dynamical systems framework for describing formation of topological charges. This attitude provides a direct link between polarization vortex and the local structure of the vector polarization field. Within the proposed framework, we challenge the established identification of the topological charge with the Hopf index of the dominant multipole and demonstrate the significant role played by derivatives of the multipolar coefficients in determining the charge. Our theoretical framework is validated within semi-analytical multipolar decompositions and full-wave numerical simulations of periodic dielectric metasurfaces. Furthermore, we show how the symmetry of the unit cell influences the local structure of the polarization field around BIC and identify the necessary conditions for the formation of high topological charges. Our findings provide a more rigorous basis for analysing BICs' topological properties, paving the way for advanced applications in topological photonics.
tldr: The paper develops a dynamical-systems framework to predict the topological charges of bound states in the continuum (BICs) in periodic dielectric metasurfaces, showing that derivatives of multipolar coefficients—not just the dominant multipole's Hopf index—determine the charge.
motivation: Conventional multipolar formalisms fail to predict BIC topological charges when no single multipole dominates the mode, and controlling these charges is essential for topological photonics.
method: A rigorous dynamical-systems treatment linking polarization vortices to the local structure of the vector polarization field, validated with semi-analytical multipolar decompositions and full-wave numerical simulations of metasurfaces.
result: The established identification of topological charge with the dominant multipole's Hopf index is challenged, derivatives of multipolar coefficients are shown to matter, and symmetry-dependent conditions for high topological charges are identified.
conclusion: The framework offers a more rigorous basis for analyzing BIC topological properties and enables advanced applications in topological photonics.

title: Don't Blame The Model, Verify The Data: An Evaluation Of SMT-based Dataset Verification
authors: Sehee Park, Dominik Gei{\ss}ler, Andrei Aleksandrov, Kim V\"ollinger
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20959v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The EU AI Act mandates that datasets for high-risk machine learning (ML) systems meet strict quality criteria such as soundness and bias mitigation. While Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT) solving offers a formal approach to verifying these properties, its scalability in realistic ML settings remains unexplored. To bridge this gap, this work presents the first large-scale empirical study of SMT-based dataset verification on two real-world ML datasets. We systematically evaluate how solver performance is shaped by three key dimensions: the type of data-quality property, the specification style, and the dataset encoding strategy. Our findings demonstrate that SMT-based verification is feasible for practical scenarios, but each dimension shapes it: the property type sets the tractability limit, the specification style drives scalability (exceeding 2000x for aggregate properties), and the encoding strategy has a systematic effect, with extracted feature columns performing best.
tldr: A large-scale empirical study of SMT-based verification of data-quality properties in real-world ML datasets, examining how property type, specification style, and encoding strategy affect solver scalability.
motivation: The EU AI Act requires high-risk ML datasets to satisfy formal quality criteria such as soundness and bias mitigation, and although SMT solving offers a formal verification route, its practical scalability had not been systematically studied.
method: The authors conduct the first large-scale empirical evaluation of SMT-based dataset verification on two real-world ML datasets, varying data-quality property type, specification style, and dataset encoding strategy.
result: SMT-based verification is feasible in practical scenarios; property type determines the tractability limit, specification style can change scalability by over 2000x for aggregate properties, and encoding strategy has a systematic effect with extracted feature columns performing best.
conclusion: SMT-based dataset verification is a viable tool for regulatory compliance of ML datasets, but performance is strongly shaped by design choices in property specification and encoding.

title: A CSFG-based Neural Network Basis-selection Method For Large-scale Rci Calculations Within Graspg
authors: Chaofan Shi, Shaowei Tian, Ran Si, Gediminas Gaigalas, Per J\"onsson, Chongyang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a neural network (NN) basis-selection method for large-scale relativistic configuration interaction (RCI) calculations in GRASPG. The method employs configuration state function generators (CSFGs), each of which generates a set of configuration state functions (CSFs) with the same spin-angular couplings, as the basic selection units for the NN. A constant-orbital feature-elimination strategy removes feature channels whose values remain unchanged across the CSFG pool. The CSFG representation reduces the number of learning units processed by the NN by more than one order of magnitude, while constant-orbital feature elimination further reduces the dimensionality of the NN input. Combined with the high-performance GRASPG framework, the method improves the efficiency of both NN selection and subsequent RCI calculations, maintaining a balance between accuracy and computational cost. In a moderate Ni(12+) benchmark, where the corresponding full-space RCI calculation is still feasible, the CSFs generated by the retained CSFG sets reproduce the full-space RCI results at the few inverse-centimeter level for the target states. For the representative J = 0, even-parity block, the complete workflow reduces the wall time by 75.6 percent, and the peak memory required by a single RCI calculation is reduced by a factor of 10.1. In a larger-scale calculation with a full CSF expansion containing 1.27 x 10^9 CSFs, the method retains only 1.1-1.9 percent of the full-space CSFs and yields energy levels in good agreement with experimental data and other resource-intensive theoretical calculations.

motivation: Large-scale RCI calculations for highly charged ions suffer from prohibitively large CSF expansions, so efficient selection of the dominant CSFs is needed to balance accuracy against computational cost.
method: CSFG blocks (sets of CSFs sharing spin-angular coupling) serve as the neural network's selection units, combined with a constant-orbital feature-elimination strategy to cut input dimensionality, all integrated into the high-performance GRASPG framework.
result: In a Ni(12+) benchmark, retained CSFGs reproduce full-space RCI energies to within a few inverse centimeters, reducing wall time by 75.6% and peak memory by 10.1x; a 1.27e9-CSF expansion is compressed to 1.1-1.9% of CSFs with levels still matching experiment.
conclusion: The CSFG-based NN selection yields accurate atomic energy levels at drastically reduced computational cost, enabling RCI calculations at scales previously infeasible.

title: Gradient Nature Of Laplacian Growth

motivation: Laplacian growth processes appear in diverse physical contexts, and the author aims to uncover a variational/gradient structure underlying their boundary dynamics.
method: The work uses methods from complex analysis and the geometry of curve spaces, showing that the boundary motion follows the gradient of a functional on smooth closed curves.
result: For a class of Laplacian growth processes, the growing domain's boundary moves along the gradient of a functional, which in the simplest cases is given by the external conformal radius.

title: The Charge Dependent Hard-sphere Model: Polycrystals As Low-energy Configurations
authors: Timo Ziereis Leonard Kreutz
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the emergence of rigid polycrystalline structures in atomistic ionic particle systems as low-energy configurations. The interaction between particles of opposite charge is modeled by hard spheres that interact when they are tangential. The interaction between particles of same charge is modeled as a hard repulsion that forces a minimal distance between them. The atomistic energy is frame invariant, and no underlying reference lattice is assumed on the ionic configurations. The asymptotic behavior of configurations with finite surface energy scaling is identified by means of [MATH]-convergence. The related continuum theory is described by piecewise constant fields that encode the local orientation of the configuration. The limiting energy is local and concentrates at grain boundaries, which correspond to the boundaries of the regions where the underlying configuration has a constant orientation. The limiting energy density is anisotropic and depends on the relative misorientation of the two grains, their translation misfit, and the normal to their interface. Furthermore, we perform a fine analysis of surface energies for solid-solid and solid-vacuum phase transitions and determine energetically favorable orientation mismatches. This relies on a structure result for our grain boundaries, which shows that, due to the rigid setup, interpolating layers near the grain interface are energetically not favorable.
tldr: The paper derives a continuum theory for rigid polycrystalline structures emerging as low-energy configurations in charge-dependent hard-sphere atomistic systems via Gamma-convergence.
motivation: To understand how polycrystalline order arises in ionic particle systems without assuming an underlying reference lattice, using a minimal hard-sphere interaction model.
method: Opposite charges are modeled as tangential hard spheres and same charges as hard repulsion enforcing a minimal distance; Gamma-convergence is applied to identify asymptotic surface energy scaling and the limiting continuum energy.
result: The limiting energy is local, concentrated at grain boundaries, and anisotropic, depending on grain misorientation, translation misfit, and interface normal; favorable orientation mismatches are determined under a grain-boundary structure result.
conclusion: The work rigorously links atomistic charge-dependent hard-sphere interactions to a polycrystal continuum model and shows that interpolating layers near grain interfaces are energetically unfavorable due to the rigid setup.

title: Cotensor Decompositions For Comodules Over Graded Vertex Operator Coalgebras

motivation: The work aims to develop a coalgebraic representation theory for vertex operator coalgebras, likely motivated by mathematical structures in conformal field theory and their dualities.
method: It introduces contragredient comodules and cointertwining operators, then defines cotensor decompositions via a universal property and proves the coalgebra structure of the Grothendieck group.
result: The complexified Grothendieck group of admissible comodules is shown to be a cocommutative coassociative coalgebra naturally dual to the fusion algebra of admissible modules over the dual vertex operator algebra.
conclusion: The paper provides a formal coalgebraic framework for vertex operator coalgebras, advancing pure algebraic representation theory but not directly connecting to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: SpaceDiffusion: Over-the-Orbit Diffusion For Space Generate-and-Forward Communications
authors: Jianhao Huang, Zhanwei Wang, Khaled B. Letaief, Kaibin Huang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.20899v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Satellite communications are an essential component of sixth-generation (6G) mobile networks, which provide ubiquitous connectivity for global services. However, the satellite uplink remains a critical bottleneck for ground devices: their limited transmit power and antenna apertures result in low data rates and high packet errors. To overcome this bottleneck, this paper advocates a novel relaying paradigm termed generate-and-forward (GF) communications, where satellites exploit on-orbit generative artificial intelligence (AI) to robustly reconstruct corrupted data prior to forwarding. Specifically, we propose SpaceDiffusion, an over-the-orbit diffusion framework for satellite-assisted image transmission. The core of this framework is a channel-distortion-aware diffusion theory developed using the following approach. By formulating the recovery of compressed and lost image tokens as an inverse problem, this theory incorporates a channel-distortion correction term directly into the conventional denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM) update. As a result, this design enables a single pretrained diffusion model to adapt dynamically to varying packet-loss patterns and compression distortions without retraining. Furthermore, we analytically characterize the progressive token-reconstruction error and derive a diffusion-step activation threshold that predicts when SpaceDiffusion is expected to outperform conventional decode-and-forward (DF) relaying. Building on these theoretical insights, we further develop an energy-aware early-exit policy to efficiently deploy SpaceDiffusion in orbit. Experimental results demonstrate that SpaceDiffusion achieves lower end-to-end latency compared to DF scheme with retransmission protocol and saves approximately 15 dB of uplink transmit power at a target perceptual quality.
tldr: The paper proposes SpaceDiffusion, an over-the-orbit diffusion framework for satellite-assisted image transmission using generate-and-forward communications.
motivation: Satellite uplinks are bottlenecked by limited ground-device transmit power and antenna apertures, causing low data rates and high packet errors in 6G networks.
method: It formulates image-token recovery as an inverse problem and incorporates a channel-distortion correction term into DDIM updates, enabling a pretrained diffusion model to adapt to packet loss and compression without retraining.
result: SpaceDiffusion achieves lower end-to-end latency than decode-and-forward with retransmission and saves approximately 15 dB of uplink transmit power at a target perceptual quality.
conclusion: On-orbit generative AI relaying can robustly reconstruct corrupted data and improve satellite communication efficiency, though the work is outside quantum information research.

title: Bounds On The Semidefinite Programming Complexity Of The Euclidean Ball

abstract: ArXiv:2609.21089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present tight lower bounds for the size of any linear matrix inequality representation of the Euclidean ball, and on the semidefinite extension complexity of the ball. method: The authors use elementary facts about the dimension of the set of faces of spectrahedra, extending the arguments to convex sets whose extreme points form a semialgebraic set.

title: Spectral Deflation For Factorization-Free Matrix Filtering In Muon And Semidefinite Programming
authors: Haoran Sun, Shucheng Kang, Heng Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21102v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: GPU implementations of the Muon optimizer and of first-order semidefinite programming (SDP) solvers share one computational pattern: a matrix factorization is replaced by a fixed-depth polynomial filter applied after normalization. When a few dominant spectral components carry most of the input's scale, normalization pushes the remaining spectrum toward zero, where the filter is least accurate. We propose spectral deflation: estimate the dominant components, remove them, filter the normalized residual with the unchanged filter, and restore them. Deflation preserves the target matrix function, and we prove that it strictly reduces the finite-step error of the classical Newton--Schulz family. Implemented with batched randomized SVD for Muon and warm-started subspace tracking for ADMM, deflation consistently improves GPT-2 pretraining over the corresponding Muon baselines with both the Newton--Schulz and Polar Express mappings, also in wall-clock time, and lowers the KKT residuals of factorization-free ADMM on large-scale SDPs within a similar projection time.
tldr: The paper introduces spectral deflation to improve factorization-free matrix filtering used in the Muon optimizer and first-order semidefinite programming solvers.
motivation: In GPU implementations of Muon and ADMM-based SDP solvers, replacing matrix factorization with fixed-depth polynomial filters after normalization is inaccurate when a few dominant spectral components dominate the input scale.
method: The authors estimate and remove dominant spectral components, filter the normalized residual with the unchanged filter, and then restore the removed components, using batched randomized SVD for Muon and warm-started subspace tracking for ADMM.
result: Spectral deflation consistently improves GPT-2 pretraining over Muon baselines with Newton-Schulz and Polar Express mappings, including wall-clock time, and lowers KKT residuals of factorization-free ADMM on large-scale SDPs.
conclusion: Deflation preserves the target matrix function and strictly reduces the finite-step error of the classical Newton-Schulz family, offering a practical enhancement for factorization-free matrix filtering.

title: The Manifold Hypothesis Under Unknown Gaussian Noise:Conditional Certificates And Consistent Dimension Estimation

conclusion: The work provides rigorous statistical guarantees for manifold dimension estimation under noise, with explicit limits illustrated by exact Cantor-set calculations.

title: Order Isomorphisms On Positive Cones Of Non-unital $C^*$-algebras

title: Explicit Constructions Of Maximum-Cardinality Families Of Plateaued Functions With Pairwise Disjoint Walsh Supports

title: Orbital Detection: On Maximum-Entropy Priors
authors: Kuranage Roche Rayan Ranasinghe, Takumi Takahashi, Giuseppe Thadeu Freitas de Abreu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Soft-input detection over a discrete constellation \(\) of cardinality \(M\) requires computing a posterior whose mean and mode are respectively given by the minimum mean square error (MMSE) and maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimates, both of which incur a computational cost of order \((M)\) per symbol. We show that this cost is reduced to \((L)\), where \(L \le M\) is the number of distinct amplitudes (rings), once the discrete prior is replaced by its maximum-entropy counterpart subject to the same radial marginal. This orbital prior, which is a mixture of uniform circular shells, is obtained by maximizing a mixed discrete-continuous entropy. We prove in this paper that such a distribution is the only distribution on \(\) that preserves the amplitude statistics of \(\) exactly while remaining maximally noncommittal in phase. Under the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, the orbital prior induces a closed-form posterior that factors into a softmax over the \(L\) rings and a von Mises phase distribution whose concentration is supplied entirely by the observation, yielding closed-form orbital MMSE and MAP detectors of the discrete symbol at \((L)\) cost. The resulting hierarchical rule selects the ring by posterior mass and the phase by conditional mode. We compare the pairwise ring boundary with that of the joint posterior-density and quantify the leading-order outward shift at high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Numerical results using standard constellations confirm that the orbital detectors maintain similar symbol error rate (SER) performance to optimal detectors, at a fraction of the complexity.

motivation: Soft-input detection over discrete constellations with cardinality M requires costly computation of MMSE and MAP estimates, motivating lower-complexity alternatives that preserve detection accuracy.
method: The discrete prior is replaced by a maximum-entropy distribution preserving the radial marginal, yielding a mixture of uniform circular shells; under AWGN, the posterior factors into a softmax over rings and a von Mises phase distribution, giving closed-form orbital MMSE and MAP detectors.
result: The orbital detectors achieve O(L) complexity and, in numerical experiments with standard constellations, maintain SER performance comparable to optimal detectors at a fraction of the cost.
conclusion: A maximum-entropy orbital prior enables efficient hierarchical ring-phase detection, with a quantified leading-order boundary shift at high SNR, offering a practical complexity reduction for constellation detection.

title: Dense Times-b Orbits From Times-a Invariant Sets And Measures, In Zero Entropy

title: Riesz Sequences Near The Critical Density
authors: Jordy Timo van Velthoven Marcin Bownik
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21589v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We construct Riesz sequences whose Beurling density is arbitrary close to the critical density in the setting of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces on metric measure spaces. In particular, our results apply to exponential systems on unbounded sets, nonlocalized Gabor systems and general coherent systems arising from nilpotent Lie groups. motivation: The critical density problem for Riesz sequences is a fundamental question in frame theory and sampling, with connections to Weaver's conjecture and the redundancy of frames.
method: The authors use methods from their previous work on frame redundancy and a selector form of Weaver's conjecture to build Riesz sequences near critical density in abstract reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces.

title: Parameter Estimation For Graphon-interacting Particle Systems From Discrete Observations

title: Connections Between Quadratic Transform For Fractional Programming And Schur Complement
authors: Kaiming Shen, Kareem M. Attiah, Yannan Chen, Wei Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21730v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper shows that there are intimate connections between the quadratic transform technique for solving fractional programming (FP) problems and the Schur-complement technique in matrix analysis. We demonstrate that the quadratic transform technique is related to two aspects of the Schur complement: (i) the linear matrix inequality (LMI) condition for positive semidefiniteness and (ii) the matrix determinant formula. Specifically, we establish that the quadratic transform and the Schur-complement LMI condition imply each other. This connection allows us to provide new interpretations of the auxiliary variable in the quadratic transform, and it allows us to rederive the Schur-complement determinant formula. Furthermore, this connection leads to generalizations of the quadratic transform in FP and the Schur-complement LMI that can accommodate generalized matrix inverse. As an application in information theory, we apply the generalized FP framework to the least-favorable-noise minimax formulation of the Gaussian vector broadcast channel sum capacity problem. When the least-favorable noise covariance is singular, matrix-inverse-based Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) analysis would require a careful analysis of the input and output spaces of the channel. We show using generalized FP that an auxiliary-variable representation of the singular matrix fraction directly yields the reciprocal multiple-access channel and recovers the uplink-downlink duality relation for sum capacity.
tldr: The paper connects quadratic transform for fractional programming with Schur complement techniques, applying generalized results to Gaussian vector broadcast channel sum capacity and uplink-downlink duality.
motivation: Fractional programming and Schur complements are powerful tools in optimization and information theory, but their underlying relationship has not been fully clarified, especially for singular matrix cases.
method: The authors establish mutual implications between the quadratic transform and the Schur-complement LMI condition, reinterpret the auxiliary variable, and generalize both frameworks to use generalized matrix inverses.
result: They show that the generalized FP framework directly yields the reciprocal multiple-access channel and recovers uplink-downlink duality for sum capacity even when the least-favorable noise covariance is singular.
conclusion: The work provides a unified optimization-theoretic perspective that avoids delicate KKT analysis of singular cases and offers new interpretations of auxiliary variables in fractional programming.

title: NetInspector: Measuring And Improving Llm Capabilities For Reliable Intent-Based Networking Policy Generation
authors: Yuxuan Zhang, Hongxin Hu, Guofei Gu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21103v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern networks are large in scale and heterogeneous in configuration, making manual policy management increasingly impractical. Intent-Based Networking (IBN) addresses this by automating the translation of high-level operator goals into low-level network configurations. Yet existing IBN systems rely on static heuristics and fixed-feature classifiers that generalize poorly to distribution shifts such as new service definitions or evolving phrasing in operator requests. Large Language Models (LLMs), with strong reasoning and translation capabilities demonstrated across many domains, are a natural candidate for IBN policy generation. However, it is unclear whether LLMs can be reliably applied to this task, nor whether their use mitigates or worsens the underlying security risk. In this work, we show that while fine-tuned LLMs excel at intent translation, they exhibit false negative rates when checking whether a proposed intent violates an existing security policy. The root cause is not a lack of logical reasoning capability, but LLMs lack of persistent grounding in network topology and group hierarchy. Motivated by this finding, we introduce NetInspector, a three-layer agentic framework that enforces a verify-then-act protocol, decoupling information retrieval from reasoning so that the LLM focuses on symbolic reasoning while every policy decision is grounded in verifiable network facts retrieved from a live Environment Layer before approval. On NetInspector-Bench, a 2,224-sample synthetic benchmark spanning campus, enterprise, and WAN topologies, NetInspector reduces FNR by over 30\% relative to ungrounded baselines and remains robust under linguistic distribution shifts.
tldr: NetInspector is a three-layer agentic framework that improves LLM-based intent-based networking policy generation by grounding decisions in verifiable network facts, reducing false negative rates in security policy checks.
motivation: Existing intent-based networking systems rely on static heuristics and fixed-feature classifiers that generalize poorly to distribution shifts, and it is unclear whether LLMs can be reliably applied without worsening security risks.
method: The authors fine-tune LLMs for intent translation and introduce NetInspector, which enforces a verify-then-act protocol, decoupling information retrieval from reasoning so the LLM focuses on symbolic reasoning while policy decisions are grounded in live network facts.
result: On NetInspector-Bench, a 2,224-sample synthetic benchmark, NetInspector reduces the false negative rate by over 30% relative to ungrounded baselines and remains robust under linguistic distribution shifts.
conclusion: Grounding LLMs in persistent network topology and group hierarchy is key to reliable and secure intent-based networking policy generation.

title: Fooling Thresholds Of Halfspaces
authors: Minglong Qin, Penghui Yao, Mingnan Zhao, Haigang Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We initiate the study of constructing explicit pseudorandom generators for thresholds of halfspaces with seed length polylogarithmic in the number of halfspaces. This class of functions lies at the frontier of circuit complexity [CTW26]. We show that the generator designed by O'Donnell, Servedio, and Tan for polytopes [OST22] also fools this broader class. To analyze the generator, we develop a threshold-specific smooth approximation framework based on a Bentkus-type mollifier. We prove derivative bounds for this mollifier and also establish a Boolean anticoncentration theorem for thresholds of halfspaces via a random thinning argument. These ingredients imply that the generator [MATH]-fools every [MATH]-out-of-[MATH] threshold of [MATH] halfspaces over [MATH] with seed length [MATH], for any arbitrarily small constant [MATH], where [MATH]. The random thinning argument also yields bounds on the noise sensitivity and Gaussian surface area for thresholds of halfspaces, leading to learning algorithms under both the uniform and Gaussian distributions.
tldr: The paper constructs explicit pseudorandom generators for thresholds of halfspaces with polylogarithmic seed length, using a threshold-specific smooth approximation and Boolean anticoncentration theorem.
motivation: Thresholds of halfspaces are a frontier class in circuit complexity, and explicit pseudorandom generators with short seed length are sought for derandomization and learning.
method: The authors analyze the O'Donnell-Servedio-Tan generator for polytopes and extend it to thresholds of halfspaces via a Bentkus-type mollifier, derivative bounds, and a random thinning argument.
result: They obtain a generator that fools every k-out-of-n threshold of m halfspaces over the Boolean cube with seed length polylogarithmic in the number of halfspaces, and also derive noise sensitivity and Gaussian surface area bounds leading to learning algorithms under uniform and Gaussian distributions.
conclusion: The work initiates the study of explicit PRGs for thresholds of halfspaces, providing a smooth approximation framework and anticoncentration tools with implications for learning theory.

title: Conformal Privacy Auditing: Calibrated Re-identification Attacks With Statistical Guarantees
authors: Shuo Huang, Gholamreza Haffari, Xingliang Yuan, Ting Yu, Lizhen Qu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21340v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Empirical identity leakage from released text is increasingly driven by attackers that combine large language models (LLMs) with auxiliary knowledge to link documents to individuals. Existing audits typically report success rates for specific attack pipelines but lack finite-sample statistical guarantees, while training-time protections such as differential privacy are difficult to translate into release-time decisions for individual natural-language documents. We introduce Conformal Privacy Auditing(CPA), a distribution-free calibration framework that provides a statistical certificate of re-identification risk for each released document against LLM-empowered adversaries. CPA outputs a conformal ambiguity set of candidate identities that is guaranteed to contain the true identity with user-chosen confidence under exchangeability, together with an interpretable leakage proxy derived from set size. CPA supports both logit-access and sampling-only attackers, enabling audits of open-source models and proprietary API models in a unified framework. Across multiple release benchmarks and attacker configurations, CPA achieves calibrated coverage and reveals sharp shifts in certified identifiability as auxiliary knowledge, LLM augmentation, and release mechanisms vary, providing a statistically grounded basis for reporting and comparing release-time linkage risk across attacker configurations, datasets, and release mechanisms alike.
tldr: CPA is a distribution-free conformal calibration framework that provides statistical certificates of re-identification risk for released text against LLM-empowered adversaries.
motivation: Empirical identity leakage from released text is increasingly driven by LLM-based attackers, but existing audits lack finite-sample statistical guarantees and differential privacy is difficult to apply at release time for individual documents.
method: CPA outputs a conformal ambiguity set of candidate identities guaranteed to contain the true identity with user-chosen confidence under exchangeability, along with an interpretable leakage proxy from set size, supporting both logit-access and sampling-only attackers.
result: Across multiple release benchmarks and attacker configurations, CPA achieves calibrated coverage and reveals sharp shifts in certified identifiability as auxiliary knowledge, LLM augmentation, and release mechanisms vary.
conclusion: CPA provides a statistically grounded basis for reporting and comparing release-time linkage risk across attacker configurations, datasets, and release mechanisms.

title: CESBench: Benchmarking Large Language Models On Cryptographic Engineering Security For IoT Devices
authors: Wenquan Zhou, An Wang, Jing Liang, Peien Feng, Jingqi Zhang, Yaoling Ding, Liehuang Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For Internet of Things (IoT) devices, a secure algorithm alone is not enough: an attacker with physical access can attack the implementation directly, and its flaws are hard to fix once deployed. Large language models (LLMs) are now used to build and analyze such implementations. LLM benchmarks exist for cryptography and general cybersecurity, but none covers cryptographic engineering. In this paper, we present CESBench, 380 expert-written items across six sub-domains of cryptographic engineering security for IoT devices: side-channel, fault injection, implementation, countermeasures, evaluation, and integration. Four task types target different competences: 209 multiple-choice items test recall, 67 judgment items require a security verdict and its justification, 63 scenario items require an engineering diagnosis, and 41 code tasks are graded by 572 test cases. To validate the benchmark, 11 open-weight and proprietary LLMs answer every item. Multiple-choice and code responses are scored automatically, and judgment and scenario responses by an LLM judge, whose scores are checked against a second judge from another model family and human re-scoring. Composite scores range from 54.4% to 83.6%. The top score on each task type is 98.6% for multiple choice, 95.1% for code, and 88.4% for scenario diagnosis, but only 58.8% for judgment. Across models, 88.5% of verdicts are correct, yet their justifications earn only 53.4% of the rubric marks. Multiple choice is near its ceiling for the strongest models and most code tasks are solved, whereas justifying a security verdict remains the weakest competence. The benchmark, prompts, and per-item results are public.
tldr: CESBench is a benchmark of 380 expert-written items for evaluating large language models on cryptographic engineering security for IoT devices.
motivation: While LLMs are increasingly used to build and analyze IoT cryptographic implementations, existing benchmarks cover cryptography or general cybersecurity but not cryptographic engineering security, where physical attacks on implementations are critical.
method: The benchmark spans six sub-domains and four task types—multiple-choice, judgment, scenario, and code—with automatic scoring for objective items and LLM-judge plus human cross-checking for open-ended responses.
result: Across 11 LLMs, composite scores range from 54.4% to 83.6%; multiple-choice and code tasks are nearly saturated, while judgment tasks remain weakest, with correct verdicts often lacking well-scored justifications.
conclusion: CESBench fills a gap in LLM evaluation for cryptographic engineering and highlights that justifying security verdicts is the most challenging competence for current models.

title: Critical Sets Of Latin Squares Based On Autoparatopisms
authors: Manuel Gonz\'alez-Regadera, Ra\'ul M. Falc\'on, Mar\'ia Dolores Frau
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21532v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cryptography, critical sets of Latin squares have particularly been implemented to design secret sharing schemes. A main problem in these cryptographic protocols arises from absent holders of pieces of information that are common to different critical sets, because they become indispensable to recover the secret. This paper solves this problem by making use of the orbits of entries described by the autoparatopism group of the Latin square under consideration. To this end, we introduce the more general problem of computing critical sets of Latin squares having a given paratopism in their autoparatopism group. These critical sets depend only on the conjugacy class of the autoparatopism and the main class of the Latin square under consideration. Based on this fact, as an illustrative example, we determine the smallest and largest sizes of critical sets associated with autoparatopisms of Latin squares of order up to six. We implement this approach in the design of a new secret sharing scheme.
tldr: The paper studies critical sets of Latin squares using autoparatopism groups to solve a problem in secret sharing schemes where absent holders of common information become indispensable.
motivation: Critical sets of Latin squares are used in cryptographic secret sharing, but a practical problem arises when holders absent from multiple critical sets become indispensable to recover the secret.
method: The authors introduce the general problem of computing critical sets of Latin squares that have a given paratopism in their autoparatopism group, showing these critical sets depend only on the conjugacy class of the autoparatopism and the main class of the Latin square.
result: As an example, they determine the smallest and largest sizes of critical sets associated with autoparatopisms for Latin squares of order up to six, and implement the approach in a new secret sharing scheme.
conclusion: The autoparatopism-orbit approach provides a systematic way to design secret sharing schemes based on Latin squares and addresses the problem of indispensable holders.

title: RTLViT: Real-time Lensless Reconstruction With A Lightweight Vision Transformer
authors: Leyla A. Kabuli, Vasilisa Ponomarenko, Laura Waller
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21042v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mask-based lensless imagers capture measurements using simple, compact hardware and recover images using a reconstruction algorithm. The reconstruction algorithm affects the image quality, inference speed, and computational requirements of the imaging system, often trading off image quality against computational efficiency. Advancing toward integrated lensless imagers, where encoding and reconstruction occur within a single device (e.g., a mobile phone), requires a fast, high-quality, and practical reconstruction method. We introduce the Real-Time Lensless Vision Transformer (RTLViT), a lightweight, purely data-driven reconstruction architecture for high-quality and real-time lensless reconstruction. With only 1.09 million learnable parameters, RTLViT provides higher-quality reconstructions than both real-time baselines and substantially larger attention-based architectures, including improvements of up to 3.46 dB in peak signal-to-noise ratio over architectures with [MATH] more learnable parameters. We demonstrate that RTLViT maintains high-quality reconstructions across a wide range of training dataset sizes and two different mask designs (lenslets and a diffuser). Finally, we implement real-time reconstruction with RTLViT on laptops and smartphones, supporting future integrated lensless imagers for real-time applications.
tldr: RTLViT is a lightweight vision-transformer architecture (1.09M parameters) that achieves high-quality, real-time lensless image reconstruction on laptops and smartphones.
motivation: Mask-based lensless imagers need reconstruction algorithms that balance image quality against computational cost, and integrated on-device imagers require fast, practical, high-quality reconstruction.
method: The authors design a purely data-driven Vision Transformer reconstruction network with a compact parameter budget, trained and evaluated across varying dataset sizes and two mask designs (lenslets and diffuser).
result: RTLViT outperforms real-time baselines and much larger attention-based models, improving PSNR by up to 3.46 dB while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters, and runs in real time on laptops and smartphones.
conclusion: The work supports future integrated lensless imaging systems by demonstrating that lightweight transformers can deliver real-time, high-quality computational imaging on consumer hardware.

title: Topological Optical Frequency Combs
authors: Wenfu Zhang Rujiang Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21375v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optical frequency combs (OFCs) are revolutionary light sources characterized by discrete and equally spaced spectral lines, and they have found widespread applications in metrology, spectroscopy, and communications. In the early stages, OFCs were realized using mode-locked lasers. With advancements in the fabrication of high-quality factor ([MATH]) microresonators and the increasing demand for miniaturized and integrable photonic chips, microresonator-based OFCs, commonly referred to as microcombs, have been developed. Although early studies of microcombs primarily focused on single microresonators or a few resonators, a significant breakthrough occurred in 2021 when it was theoretically predicted that light propagating in the topological edge channel of an array of ring resonators could generate nested frequency combs known as topological OFCs. Since then, the field of topological OFCs has progressed rapidly, with experimental observations made in 2024. This Perspective will introduce the history of OFCs, placing particular emphasis on the emergence and development of topological OFCs, as well as exploring the research challenges and opportunities associated with them.
tldr: A Perspective reviewing the history and development of optical frequency combs, with emphasis on topological optical frequency combs generated in arrays of ring resonators.
motivation: Optical frequency combs are important for metrology, spectroscopy, and communications, and microresonator-based combs enable miniaturized integrated photonic chips. Topological edge channels offer a new route to generate nested frequency combs.
method: This is a Perspective/review article, not a primary research result; it surveys the field from mode-locked lasers to microcombs and discusses theoretical predictions and subsequent experimental observations.
result: The paper describes how light propagating in topological edge channels of ring-resonator arrays can generate nested frequency combs, a concept predicted in 2021 and experimentally observed in 2024.
conclusion: Topological optical frequency combs have progressed rapidly, and the Perspective outlines associated research challenges and opportunities.

title: Uniform Chebyshev Asymptotics For Repeated-pole Rational Approximation Of The Exponential
authors: Tianqi Zhang Fei Xue
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21028v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study uniform approximation of [MATH], [MATH], on [MATH] by rational functions [MATH] with a prescribed repeated pole [MATH]. A M\"obius transformation reduces the problem to polynomial approximation of [MATH] on [MATH], where [MATH]. We derive a uniform two-saddle asymptotic formula for the Chebyshev coefficients, including explicit amplitude and phase and a relative remainder for each localized complex saddle contribution, covering fixed, sublinear, and linear pole scalings away from saddle coalescence. Because the two saddle contributions can cancel in a single coefficient, we pass to a growing block of neighboring coefficients and prove that the whole block cannot cancel. This transfers the coefficient asymptotics to approximation errors. For [MATH], [MATH], the best uniform error has two-sided order [MATH]; at the optimal ratio [MATH] this becomes [MATH]. The normalized Chebyshev-weighted [MATH] projection error has an explicit bounded oscillatory profile. These prefactor-resolved estimates yield a two-term precision-to-work law and quantify mismatch between pole-design and stopping degrees. Finally, the scalar error gives an exact worst-case matrix-action benchmark for self-adjoint negative semidefinite matrices and dimension-independent shift-and-invert Krylov bounds.
tldr: The paper derives uniform Chebyshev asymptotics for repeated-pole rational approximation of the exponential, with implications for matrix-function benchmarks and Krylov bounds.
motivation: The authors aim to quantify sharp approximation errors for rational approximations of exp with prescribed repeated poles, motivated by understanding optimal pole design and matrix-action precision.
method: They apply a Möbius transformation to reduce the problem to polynomial approximation, then use a two-saddle asymptotic analysis of Chebyshev coefficients and a growing-block argument to transfer coefficient asymptotics to approximation errors.
result: They obtain two-sided error orders, an explicit oscillatory projection-error profile at the optimal pole ratio, a two-term precision-to-work law, and a worst-case matrix-action benchmark for self-adjoint negative semidefinite matrices.
conclusion: The work provides refined asymptotic approximation theory for exponential rational approximation and dimension-independent shift-and-invert Krylov bounds, but it is not directly related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: A Low-rank Adi Algorithm For The Numerical Solution Of Large Discrete-time Non-symmetric Algebraic Riccati Equations
authors: Umair Zulfiqar
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21282v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete-time non-symmetric algebraic Riccati equations (DTNAREs) arise in game-theoretic computations of Nash equilibria. Solving such equations at large scale is often computationally prohibitive. This paper develops a numerical approach for large-scale DTNAREs whose solutions are low rank. A low-rank alternating direction implicit (ADI) method is introduced that recursively constructs a low-rank stabilizing solution without explicitly solving any projected DTNARE. Through the pole-placement property of the low-rank ADI iteration, the method ensures that the implicitly solved projected DTNARE always admits a stabilizing solution. An automatic shift-generation strategy is also developed for the ADI iterations. Once an initial shift is provided, the algorithm computes the low-rank solution without further user intervention. Numerical experiments on DTNAREs with dimensions between \(10^6\) and \(10^7\) demonstrate the accuracy and efficiency of the method. The results confirm that the proposed low-rank ADI algorithm is an effective solver for large-scale DTNAREs that would otherwise be computationally prohibitive.
tldr: This paper introduces a low-rank ADI algorithm for efficiently solving large-scale discrete-time non-symmetric algebraic Riccati equations arising in game-theoretic Nash equilibrium computations.
motivation: Discrete-time non-symmetric algebraic Riccati equations (DTNAREs) appear in game-theoretic computations but become computationally prohibitive at large scales, motivating the need for specialized numerical solvers.
method: The authors develop a low-rank alternating direction implicit (ADI) method that recursively constructs a low-rank stabilizing solution without explicitly solving any projected DTNARE, and they propose an automatic shift-generation strategy for the ADI iterations.
result: Numerical experiments on DTNAREs with dimensions between 10^6 and 10^7 confirm the accuracy and efficiency of the low-rank ADI algorithm compared to existing prohibitive approaches.
conclusion: The proposed low-rank ADI algorithm provides an effective solver for large-scale DTNAREs, enabling game-theoretic computations that would otherwise be infeasible.

title: Co-Evolving Zero-Day Jamming: Adaptive Attack Synthesis And Graph Attention-Based Online Detection
authors: Ghilas Aissou, R\'emi A. Chou, Taejoon Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.21334v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Effective evaluation of zero-day jamming detectors requires robust adversarial models. However, existing attack models often assume prior knowledge of the target receiver, limiting their utility as evaluation benchmarks. On the detection side, existing detectors fail to capture the global temporal-spectral structure of jamming behavior and cannot differentiate zero-day strategies as they emerge. This paper addresses these limitations through a two-pronged framework. First, an online detection framework is introduced that combines a graph attention network (GAT) for temporal-spectral representation learning with Dirichlet process (DP)-means clustering. This framework jointly classifies known and discovers zero-day strategies within a unified learning objective. Second, an inference-driven reinforcement learning (RL) jammer is proposed as an adversarial benchmark. The jammer treats the target receiver as a black-box, infers the detector state via hypothesis testing, and optimizes the trade-off between attack impact and stealth. Simulation results show that the proposed RL jammer outperforms benchmarks, achieving 33% higher attack efficacy and 67% higher stealth. The proposed detection framework against the proposed RL jammer is shown to achieve 20% higher detection accuracy than the benchmarks.
tldr: The paper proposes a co-evolving framework pairing a graph attention network with Dirichlet-process clustering for online detection of zero-day jamming, alongside an inference-driven reinforcement-learning jammer used as an adversarial benchmark.
motivation: Existing jamming attack models assume prior knowledge of the target receiver and thus make poor evaluation benchmarks, while existing detectors cannot capture global temporal-spectral structure or identify emerging zero-day jamming strategies.
method: A graph attention network learns temporal-spectral representations that are jointly clustered via Dirichlet process means to classify known and discover novel jamming strategies in one objective; a black-box RL jammer infers the detector state by hypothesis testing and optimizes an attack-impact/stealth trade-off.
